https://iz.ru/2187795/2026-10-21/ssha-i-.body: США и Украина во вторник, 20 октября, завершили переговоры в Осло с участием представителей Евросоюза и НАТО. После них спецпосланник Белого дома Стивен Уиткофф отправился в Санкт-Петербург на встречу с президентом РФ Владимиром Путиным. Он должен передать новый план мирного урегулирования, выработанный в Норвегии. Что пишут СМИ о перспективах переговорного процесса — в дайджесте «Известий». Axios: Уиткофф представит Путину мирное предложение после переговоров с Зеленским По словам американского чиновника, специальный посланник Белого дома Стивен Уиткофф встретится с президентом России Владимиром Путиным в Санкт-Петербурге 21 октября и представит ему обновленное предложение по прекращению конфликта на Украине. Зять и советник президента США Дональда Трампа, Джаред Кушнер, примет участие во встрече в режиме онлайн. Axios Уиткофф прибудет в Россию после дня переговоров в Осло с президентом Украины Владимиром Зеленским, а также лидерами Норвегии и Финляндии и представителями Франции, Великобритании, Германии, Польши, ЕС и НАТО. Обсуждения в Осло были сосредоточены на разработке единого предложения по «рамочному соглашению» о прекращении конфликта. Американский чиновник заявил, что Украина «выдвинула новые идеи и предложения, которые были подробно обсуждены». Он добавил, что стороны добились «значительного прогресса» и теперь имеют «твердое согласие на рабочем уровне» относительно дальнейших шагов. Reuters: Трамп подталкивает Киев к урегулированию По словам представителя США, Украина представила на переговорах в Осло, в которых участвовали лидеры Норвегии и Финляндии, а также представители Европы и НАТО, новые идеи и предложения. Участники достигли «значительного прогресса» в выработке согласованного подхода к взаимодействию с Россией. Чиновник сообщил, что в ходе переговоров обсуждались «ключевые элементы комплексной мирной структуры», включая гарантии безопасности для Украины, план дальнейшего экономического восстановления и более широкую архитектуру европейской безопасности. Reuters Зеленский прибыл в Осло, стремясь наладить отношения с Вашингтоном, которые опустились до рекордно низкого уровня на фоне попыток Трампа сблизиться с Москвой. Киев выражал недовольство тем, что Вашингтон удерживает критически важную военную помощь и разведывательные данные. После переговоров Зеленский заявил, что Киев рассчитывает обсудить ключевые вопросы завершения конфликта в ходе трехсторонней встречи лидеров Украины, России и США. Премьер-министр Норвегии Йонас Гар Стёре заявил на пресс-конференции, что встреча в Осло прошла хорошо и конструктивно, а президент Финляндии Александр Стубб добавил: «Думаю, мирный процесс снова на верном пути». Трамп и Зеленский продолжают публично ссориться. Что это означает Associated Press: Зеленский заявил о получении разведданных от США Зеленский заявил в Осло, что Киев вновь получает предупреждения от своих партнеров о приближающихся ракетах. По меньшей мере неделю назад украинский лидер заявлял, что его страна не получала данных о баллистических ракетах, нацеленных на столицу. По его словам, такая информация спасает жизни, позволяя оповестить население и давая воинским частям время попытаться перехватить ракеты. Associated Press Зеленский заявил, что изменения произошли после переговоров с его американскими коллегами, включая телефонный разговор с госсекретарем США Марко Рубио. По словам Зеленского, у Украины почти закончились американские зенитные ракеты Patriot, необходимые для перехвата баллистических ракет, и он призвал Вашингтон направить больше таких боеприпасов. Он отметил, что Пентагон задерживает поставку ракет, закупленных для Украины другими странами. Украинский лидер также заявил, что в его стране по-прежнему действуют ограничения скорости при использовании Starshield, военной версии спутникового интернет-сервиса Starlink. Bloomberg: Украина не смогла бы существовать без поддержки США, заявил Рубио Госсекретарь США Марко Рубио выступил в защиту поддержки Украины со стороны администрации Трампа, заявив, что страна «не существовала бы» без поддержки США. Он заявил об этом, отвечая на вопросы о том, что генеральный директор SpaceX Илон Маск якобы распорядился замедлить работу спутниковой системы Starshield, которая помогает Украине отражать воздушные атаки. Bloomberg «Если бы не помощь Соединенных Штатов, в том числе при администрации Трампа, Украины сейчас бы не существовало, — заявил Рубио журналистам [21 октября] во время визита в Индию. — Украина как суверенное государство не существовала бы». Рубио заявил, что ему ничего не было известно о каком-либо предварительном уведомлении об отключении Starshield со стороны Трампа, и сказал, что США в любом случае не могут контролировать, что частная компания делает со своей продукцией. Госсекретарь также отметил, что сейчас ведутся «очень сложные переговоры» с целью урегулирования конфликта. По его словам, сейчас они сосредоточены на судьбе Донбасса, и были предложены некоторые «креативные идеи» для преодоления разногласий. Почему обострился конфликт между Зеленским и Трампом? Ответы на главные вопросы BBC News: Трамп и Зеленский, похоже, находятся в конфронтации Объятия, которыми Уиткофф встретил Зеленского перед переговорами в Осло, вряд ли развеяли опасения украинского лидера по поводу нынешнего курса политики США в отношении его страны. Зеленский опубликовал видео этого момента в социальных сетях, но, учитывая всё, что произошло в октябре, считает ли он Трампа по-прежнему своим партнером? Эти двое политиков никогда не были близки — это очевидно, — но не поссорились ли они теперь окончательно? BBC News Личные нападки типичны для жесткого подхода Трампа к дипломатии. Трудно понять, когда их следует воспринимать всерьез. В июне он обрушился с критикой на премьер-министра Израиля, заявив, что у Биньямина Нетаньяху «нет здравого смысла». Четыре месяца спустя он с энтузиазмом поддержал Нетаньяху, назвав его великим премьер-министром и воином. Зеленский, со своей стороны, в целом проявляет осторожность в своих высказываниях о своем ненадежном, но важном американском коллеге. Но в этом месяце его разочарование стало очевидным. Обращаясь к делегации конгресса США, он говорил о «решениях с американской стороны, которые трудно объяснить друзьям», и выразил опасение, что «было принято какое-то политическое решение, чтобы замедлить поддержку нашей стороны». Отвечая на обвинение Трампа в том, что он является главным препятствием на пути к мирному урегулированию, Зеленский звучал еще более раздраженно, чем когда-либо. Поделиться:

https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/society/.body: Home Azerbaijan Society Azerbaijan’s Press Council warns of fake journalist WhatsApp accounts Society Press release 21 October 2026 12:35 (UTC +04:00) Alish Abdulla Parliamentary Correspondent Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. The creation of fake WhatsApp accounts in the names of journalists and the subsequent sending of messages in Azerbaijan are matters of concern. This was reflected in a report published by the Press Council of Azerbaijan. According to the report, in recent days, information has been received regarding the creation of fake WhatsApp accounts in the names of well-known journalists, which are then used to send messages containing various types of content. "Statements from law enforcement agencies indicate that such activities are carried out by organized cybercriminal networks operating from outside Azerbaijan. By utilizing artificial intelligence algorithms and specialized software, these groups target civil servants, employees of various enterprises and organizations, as well as journalists and other citizens. Despite numerous awareness-raising initiatives, some citizens still fall victim to such fraudulent schemes," the council emphasized. Noting that these occurrences are not limited to isolated incidents and could potentially evolve into a concerning trend, the Press Council has urged journalists and media professionals in general to exercise caution. "It’s crucial not to trust, respond to, or share the content of suspicious messages, even if they appear to come from people they know, without first verifying their authenticity. It’s especially important to check the source and veracity of information concerning socio-political matters. It should be remembered that messages sent via fake accounts are intended to create false impressions about individuals, damage their reputations, and mislead public opinion," the statement noted. The Press Council recommended those who encounter such situations take the following steps: “- Call the Ministry of Internal Affairs' '102' service to notify law enforcement authorities. You may also contact the police station in your local area. - Reach out to the National Cybersecurity Agency. Report the incident via email at [email protected] or contact the Agency’s hotline at 1654. - Inform the public. Use your own social media accounts to make it publicly known that a fake account is operating in your name. People should know that the messages sent from that account do not come from you, and they shouldn’t accept their content as the truth. - Report the fake account to the WhatsApp platform. To do this, use the available complaint function by logging into the account profile. Keep screenshots of messages sent from the fake account, phone number, and other relevant information as evidence. In order to block the fake account, other victims can be called to file a complaint accordingly. Complaining by a minimum of 15 people is more effective. - Verify the authenticity of messages by alternative means. If you receive a suspicious message from someone you know, verify the authenticity of the information by contacting them via phone call or other known means of communication,” the report said. The report added that when journalists and other media representatives encounter such situations, they can also inform the Azerbaijan Press Council and apply to the Council for appropriate support. The Press Council called on journalists and the public to be vigilant in the digital environment, to check information sources, and not to create conditions for the spread of possible provocations carried out through fake accounts. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4237050..body: Home Azerbaijan Azerbaijan completes Horadiz-Aghband highway, railway work ongoing Azerbaijan News 20 October 2026 15:12 (UTC +04:00) Photo: State Agency of Azerbaijan Motorways Aytaj Shiraliyeva Economics Journalist Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The construction of the Horadiz-Aghband highway in Azerbaijan has been completed, while work on the railway line, part of the development of the Zangezur Corridor, is still underway. This was reflected in a statement by the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport of Azerbaijan. According to the information, efforts are also being made to modernize the railway infrastructure in Nakhchivan. "The development of the Zangezur Corridor is of particular importance for expanding Azerbaijan's transit potential and diversifying international transport routes. The development of this corridor is expected to create additional capacity for the transport of up to 15 million tons of cargo per year and strengthen regional transport links," the statement said. On August 8, 2025, following a trilateral meeting in Washington involving U.S. President Donald Trump, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan signed a joint declaration on ensuring peace between Baku and Yerevan, as well as on establishing transportation links between the main part of Azerbaijan and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. This project has been named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP). The Horadiz–Jabrayil–Zangilan–Agbhband highway is part of the Hajigabul–Horadiz–Aghband highway and the Zangezur Corridor. The total length of the project is 149.9 kilometers, of which 123.6 kilometers comprise the main section of the road. The road is built to technical category 1B standards with four to six lanes. The project includes the construction of three tunnels with a total length of 12,032 meters, 28 bridges, eight interchanges, as well as underpasses and culverts. The development of the Zangezur Corridor is aimed at expanding Azerbaijan’s transportation links with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and increasing the country’s transit capacity. https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 20 October 2026 Helena Garkava Tags Agriculture biodiversity climate change Kazakhstan Water Water Management Snow-retention techniques help farmers in Kazakhstan's Aqtöbe Region keep winter precipitation on their fields, improving soil moisture ahead of the growing season. Photo: Marina Tsygankova. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan As Kazakhstan confronts increasingly severe droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, farmers and environmental organisations are turning to relatively inexpensive methods of retaining water and restoring ecosystems. Their field experience calls into question the country’s exclusive reliance on mega hydro-engineering projects. Kazakhstan is increasingly exposed to drought, flooding and extreme heat. A severe drought hit its southern and western regions in 2021, while widespread flooding in 2024 affected much of the country. These events have intensified the debate over how Kazakhstan should adapt to a changing climate. While major water infrastructure projects form a central part of the government’s response, some farmers and conservationists argue that simpler techniques – including snow retention and soil-moisture management – also deserve attention. Their effectiveness depends on local conditions, but their relatively modest costs make them attractive in water-stressed areas. Projects in the Aqtöbe Region and efforts to restore Lake Zhumay in the Aqmola Region illustrate the potential of locally led adaptation. They also raise a broader question: how can Kazakhstan combine major infrastructure investment with approaches that retain water within landscapes? Read more on Novastan : Kazakhstan: Residents suffer from lack of water Agro-Technical Adaptation in the Aqtöbe Region Local farmers practice autumn cultivation to retain moisture in the fields, a technique also recommended as a flood-prevention measure. Marina Tsygankova, director of the “ElitAgro” public foundation in the Aqtöbe Region, considers field preparation for these purposes economically justified. According to her, combating floods by directing precipitation straight into deep soil layers at the site of snowfall is a rational strategy. The alternative would be building special moisture storage reservoirs, but such technology is significantly more expensive and complex from an engineering standpoint. In the current economic climate – where state budgets face constraints and big business is hesitant to invest – emphasis must be placed on practices accessible to the population. Mechanical snow retention remains a budget-friendly and effective solution for the dry steppe zone of Western Kazakhstan. Here, spring floods often turn into micro-disasters as rapidly melting snow rushes off fields in torrents, washing away fertile topsoil. Using tractors with snowplows and ridgers allows farmers to keep snow where it falls, protecting it from strong winds that typically blow winter precipitation into ravines and roadside ditches. Snow accumulation in Kazakhstan’s Aqtöbe Region, where farmers use snow-retention techniques to reduce runoff and improve soil moisture. Photo: Marina Tsygankova. According to observations cited by local practitioners in the Aqtöbe Region, combining snow retention with autumn cultivation can help meltwater penetrate deeper into the soil. They report moisture reaching depths of up to 110 cm, compared with 45-60 cm on untreated sloping fields, and yield gains of up to 400 kg per hectare in some drought years. These site-specific figures should not be taken as typical results across the region. Practitioners also argue that keeping snow on fields can reduce topsoil erosion and limit snowdrifts on nearby roads. Read more on Novastan : A disappearing river: the fate of the Ural Asyl Baitleuov has been farming in the Martuk District of the Aqtöbe Region for 26 years, growing barley, sorghum, wheat, and sunflower across 3,000 hectares. “We do not receive subsidies for snow retention,” Baitleuov explains. “If the snow cover is 50 to 70 centimeters, we leave it alone. Spring snowmelt plays a huge role: if it freezes at night and melts during the day, the earth absorbs the water. But if it melts around the clock, moisture washes off with the humus. We usually have a lot of snow, so we only do snow retention where accumulation is low – treating up to 500 sown hectares annually. Although costly, it generally pays off.” Snow retention has also been used to help restore a dried-up lake. Ruslan Urazaliyev, a researcher at the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan (ACBK), describes the effort at Lake Zhumay in the Aqmola Region: “For the first time, we carried out snow retention in the Qorgalzhyn District of the Aqmola Region at Lake Zhumay,” Urazaliyev recalls. “The reservoir is a key ornithological territory attracting rare birds, including the Dalmatian pelican, white-headed duck, Pallas’s gull, and greater flamingo – all listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book. Lake Zhumay also serves as a watering hole for livestock and poultry. In 2010-2011, due to a lack of moisture and high temperatures, the lake dried up completely.” At the time, ACBK was implementing a project supported by the Global Environment Facility Small Grants Programme. Local resident Timur Iskakov helped initiate a snow-retention project, working with residents during the winter of 2012-2013 to build snow barriers around the lake. ACBK’s 2013 annual report records snow depths of 80 cm in treated areas, compared with 30-40 cm on open steppe. Urazaliyev says water returned in spring 2013 and the lake’s recovery continued into 2014. He stresses that the intervention accelerated a natural process: neighbouring lakes recovered without such measures approximately two years later. Satellite views of the Lake Zhumay area in 2012, 2014 and April 2025 illustrate changes in surface water over time. Sources: Google Earth and Google Earth Timelapse, Landsat/Copernicus. Urazaliyev estimates that the work cost slightly less than 1.7 million tenge. The precise project cost and the lake-area figures cited in his account were not independently established from the historical reports reviewed for this article. “Through our actions, we accelerated the natural restoration of an 885-hectare lake,” Urazaliyev summarizes. “Later, we successfully stocked it with crucian carp to support the food chain for fish-eating birds. https://www.trend.az/casia/turkmenistan/.body: Home Central Asia Turkmenistan President Serdar Berdimuhamedov outlines gas export plans, TAPI at OGT 2026 Turkmenistan News 21 October 2026 09:44 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Press service of the President of Kazakhstan Fuad Namazov Journalist Read more ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 21. President Serdar Berdimuhamedov has highlighted plans to expand gas exports and advance the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India (TAPI) pipeline project in a congratulatory message to participants and guests of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan - 2026” (OGT 2026), which opens in Ashgabat on Wednesday, Trend 's special correspondent reports. In his message, the president said the annual forum would provide an opportunity to exchange views on priorities for developing the country’s fuel and energy sector, prospects for mutually beneficial partnerships and modern approaches to industry modernization. The accompanying exhibition, he added, would showcase innovations, advanced technologies and new projects. Berdimuhamedov highlighted the Galkynysh gas field, one of the world’s largest in terms of reserves, describing it as a key resource base for expanding Turkmenistan’s gas exports. Development of the field is proceeding in stages, with the fourth phase of industrial development launched in April 2026. The president described the launch as a historically significant step toward substantially increasing exports of natural gas. He also highlighted the TAPI gas pipeline project, which is intended to strengthen energy security and promote prosperity across the region. Development of offshore license blocks in Turkmenistan’s sector of the Caspian Sea is also continuing, building on three decades of cooperation with leading international oil and gas companies. “We will continue implementing such projects,” Berdimuhamedov said. The president also emphasized the importance of economic diversification. Turkmenistan’s National Strategy for Industrial Development for 2030-2045 is focused on hydrocarbon processing and the production of high-quality, environmentally friendly products, he noted. Berdimuhamedov stressed that neutral Turkmenistan remains open to equal and mutually beneficial partnerships, adding that foreign investors would be provided with the necessary conditions to participate in major promising projects. He expressed confidence that OGT 2026 would serve as a platform for exchanging expertise between Turkmen specialists and international partners and help lay the groundwork for future cooperation. The 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan - OGT 2026” is being held on 21-23 October 2026 in Ashgabat under the motto “Energy. Partnership. Progress.” Organised by the State Concerns Turkmengaz and Turkmennebit, the State Corporation Turkmengeology, and the Turkmen Energy Forum, it is Turkmenistan’s flagship energy event and one of the leading oil and gas forums in Eurasia. Registration closed with more than 1,700 delegates from 75 countries representing around 450 companies; the accompanying exhibition is expected to attract over 10,000 visitors and features more than 100 companies. Key themes include further development of the Galkynysh gas field (with Phase IV launched in April 2026), progress on the TAPI pipeline, Caspian offshore projects, gas processing and petrochemicals, digitalisation, methane emissions reduction, and investment opportunities. Notable partners and sponsors include SOCAR (lead/premier partner), Dragon Oil (diamond sponsor), CNPC (platinum), and Baker Hughes (silver), with Malaysia presenting its first national pavilion. And I can tell you after they violated ceasefire second time, we liberated the city of Zangilan, and many villages. So, the more time passes on the battlefield, the more territories we liberate. https://hrf.org/latest/joshua-wong-marks.body: @HRF View post Joshua Wong turned 30. He spent more than half of his twenties behind bars. From a 14-year-old student activist to one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy voices, Joshua’s story traces the dismantling of Hong Kong’s freedoms. At 14, Joshua helped organize students against a government-backed “national education” curriculum. At 17, he pushed for genuine universal suffrage. At 18, he became one of the most recognizable faces of the Umbrella Movement. He kept turning to the mechanisms available to him: peaceful protest, civil society, political organizing, and elections. One by one, those avenues closed. Since Nov. 23, 2020, Joshua has remained behind bars. He was later prosecuted alongside 46 other pro-democracy figures in the landmark “Hong Kong 47” case and sentenced to 4 years and 8 months. Then, while he was still imprisoned, authorities arrested him again in June 2025 for alleged “collusion with foreign forces.” He pleaded guilty in September 2026 and now awaits sentencing. When Joshua was first imprisoned, he noted that more than 20 political prisoners were already behind bars in Hong Kong. Today, he is one of nearly 2,000 prisoners of conscience in the city. https://www.fidh.org/en/en/region/Africa.body: 19/10/2026 Report Africa Rwanda Burundi Tanzania South Sudan Democratic Republic of Congo Ethiopia Uganda Human Rights Defenders Kayla Farmer via Unsplash A joint report by the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders -a partnership between the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH)-, the Independent Medico-legal Unit (IMLU) and SOS-Torture Burundi documents cross-border surveillance, intimidation and pressure against defenders seeking safety in the region. Brussels, Geneva, Paris, 16 October 2026. Fleeing persecution does not always mean reaching safety. A new report, Out of Reach, Not Out of Risk: Transnational Repression of Human Rights Defenders in East Africa, reveals how human rights defenders (HRDs) continue to face threats and intimidation after leaving their home countries to seek refuge elsewhere in the region. Published by the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership between the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), together with IMLU and SOS-Torture Burundi, the report draws on interviews with 50 human rights defenders from Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Ethiopia, Kenya, Sudan, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda, as well as consultations with 14 other stakeholders. It examines the risks faced by defenders living in Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda and makes recommendations to key stakeholders on prevention, protection, accountability and remedy. Repression that crosses borders Although transnational repression has long existed in Africa, it is intensifying rapidly across the continent, reaching a new peak in East Africa, where it remains poorly documented. The research highlights the interconnected nature of the risks faced by human rights defenders in East Africa, where political and security relationships, information-sharing networks and the movement of defenders between countries can allow threats to persist across borders. “ The most alarming cases show how quickly transnational repression can move from surveillance and threats to abduction, torture or other ill-treatment and attempted forcible return. States must investigate these cases, protect defenders at risk and ensure that no cooperation between governments is used to place someone at risk of torture ”, said OMCT Secretary General Stéphanie David. The report documents a range of tactics used to pressure and silence defenders beyond their countries of origin. Among the detailed threat narratives, 46% of the interviewed HRDs reported being targeted in exile, 65% involved surveillance or approaches, 30% digital targeting, 10% legal or migration-related pressure, and 10% direct physical interference. The gravest cases involved abduction, torture or other ill-treatment, enforced disappearance, and attempted unlawful removal, with host countries also playing a critical role. The report shows coordinated regional attacks among states, especially around electoral and political contests, and highlights the need to strengthen protection while carefully examining responsibility for individual incidents. “ Transnational repression in East Africa is no longer a series of isolated incidents. It is becoming increasingly regional and coordinated, with political and security cooperation allowing repression to travel across borders and follow human rights defenders into exile ”, added FIDH Vice-President Anna Henga. States must strengthen protection and accountability The report calls on states to ensure that human rights defenders can access effective protection wherever they seek refuge. It urges authorities to investigate suspected cases of transnational repression, prevent the misuse of immigration procedures and law-enforcement cooperation, and ensure that cross-border mechanisms are not used to target people for their legitimate human rights work. It also stresses the importance of early-warning mechanisms, access to remedies for victims and accountability for those responsible. The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders is a partnership between FIDH and OMCT. It works to protect human rights defenders facing risks and reprisals worldwide. OMCT and FIDH are both members of ProtectDefenders.eu, the European Union Human Rights Defenders Mechanism implemented by international civil society. https://www.rferl.org/a/moldova-russian-.body: Moldova Moldova To Probe Possible Russian Data-Harvesting After RFE/RL Investigation By Ionut Benea October 20, 2026 12:13 CET Moldova To Probe Possible Russian Data-Harvesting After RFE/RL Investigation Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A Yandex ride in the Moldovan capital, Chisinau. The company is now facing scrutiny over its operations in the country. CHISINAU -- Moldova has announced an investigation into concerns that Russian tech giant Yandex has been harvesting the personal data of its citizens by sending it directly to servers in Russia rather than storing it in the Netherlands as previously believed. The suspected data breach came to light in an investigation by RFE/RL’s Moldovan Service that revealed allegations of tax evasion by Yandex . Court files obtained by RFE/RL showed the case involved some $7.8 million in revenues from the Yandex Go taxi application allegedly flowing directly into banks in Dubai and Kazakhstan without being taxed before leaving the country. The company had refused to provide data about drivers using the app. "We understand that a large number of citizens and drivers use this platform. Therefore, we must investigate the potential risks related to the unauthorized use of personal data, through the collection, storage, processing, or unjustified access to significant volumes of personal data of citizens of the Republic of Moldova," a government statement said. SEE ALSO: How Ukraine's Strikes On Data Centers Disrupted Taxis, Shopping, And Business In Russia And Beyond Yandex is often described as "Russia's Google," though it actually sold off its search engine as part of an asset split in 2024 and provides other services, such as ride-hailing and food deliveries, that Google does not. Taken For A Ride? The Moldovan competition authority told RFE/RL that Yandex, which controls some 60 percent of the country’s taxi market, had made a $45,000 payment to the Moldovan treasury from a bank account in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on October 5. This was a fine that a company in the Yandex group, MLU BV, had received in Moldova in 2025 for refusing to provide authorities with a list of drivers using two Yandex taxi apps: Yandex Pro and Yandex Go. The former is used by taxi drivers or taxi companies, the latter by passengers. In May, MLU BV was fined $112 million in the Netherlands, where it is headquartered, on the grounds that it collected and stored customer and driver data from Norway and Finland on servers in Russia. In this case, the data included scans of driver's licenses, home addresses, contact details, account numbers, precise locations, trip history, photos, chat conversation content, and social security codes. SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy Says Yandex Strikes Crippled Pro-Kremlin Bots But Tech Experts Question Evidence Concerns have been voiced in Moldova for some years that such data is being stored in Russia. Yandex has repeatedly said that the information is kept by the group’s European companies. Moldovan authorities first requested information on drivers from Yandex back in 2022. Four such requests were made – and rejected – before, in November 2025, a fine was issued by Moldova’s competition authority to Netherlands-based Ridetech International, which ran the two Yandex applications in Moldova. By the time the fine was issued, Ridetech had been taken over by MLU BV. It responded by suing the Moldovan authority and demanding the fine be canceled. In court, MLU BV stated that Ridetech had destroyed the data. Judges said MLU BV failed to provide sufficient evidence. Court documents seen by RFE/RL do not clarify where the Moldovan drivers' data was stored or when it was deleted. The company did not respond to requests for comment. RFE/RL’s investigation was published on October 13. It also found that payments for taxi rides ordered through Yandex Go flow to a company in the UAE while Yandex Plus subscriptions are paid to a company in Kazakhstan. In June, Moldova’s parliament considered a bill obliging taxi platforms to process payments through banks within the country, but the measure did not make it to a final vote. The Fallout A day after RFE/RL’s investigation was published in Moldova, Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Bolea announced that the government would launch an inquiry into Yandex’s activities and also possible security risks. Then, on October 15, Moldova's Council for Strategic Investment Review, a government body chaired by Prime Minister Vasile Tofan, intervened. The council, which has the ability to suspend the activity of any entity deemed as a threat and has exercised these powers in the past, demanded full disclosure of the ultimate beneficiaries of Yandex's branch in Moldova and ordered personal data watchdogs to trace where user records travel. Crucially, authorities warned that the probe could lead to asset seizures or suspension of the app. It gave Yandex a 20-day deadline that the company has said it will comply with, although it did not provide details. Latvia and Estonia banned the Yandex Go app in 2022, citing security risks and the transfer of data to servers in Russia. The app is popular in multiple countries, especially in the former Soviet Union but also, for example, in Serbia. https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-russia-a.body: News Zelenskyy To Meet US Envoy Witkoff In Oslo Amid Trump Tensions And Russian Attacks By RFE/RL October 20, 2026 11:25 CET Zelenskyy To Meet US Envoy Witkoff In Oslo Amid Trump Tensions And Russian Attacks Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A woman stands at the site of her relatives' house, which was destroyed during a Russian air strike on the outskirts of Dnipro, Ukraine, on October 19. US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will take part in meetings in Oslo to discuss the situation in Ukraine with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Russia continues to pound the country amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington. The Norwegian government said in a statement that Zelenskyy would arrive in Norway on October 20 to meet with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store to put "diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path." "Ukraine has requested that US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner join the meetings," Store said. The statement added that Witkoff would travel to Oslo, while Kushner, who is ill, would participate remotely. Zelenskyy will also be received by the Norwegian king and visit the country's parliament, the statement said. Most US talks with Ukraine have involved Witkoff and Kushner and negotiators appointed by Zelenskyy, rather than the Ukrainian president himself. Neither Zelenskyy nor Russian President Vladimir Putin has attended any direct Ukraine-Russia talks aimed at ending the war. The meetings in Oslo come amid tensions between US President Donald Trump and the Ukrainian leader. Trump suggested Zelenskyy should not be involved in negotiations to end the full-scale invasion Russia launched against his country in February 2022, his latest statement in which he has voiced doubt about Zelenskyy's commitment to seeking peace. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump said. SEE ALSO: Star Wars: A Russian Military Satellite Gets Very, Very Close To One Used By Ukraine The remarks came amid concerns in Ukraine over a series of moves that Zelenskyy has said would play into Putin's hands. In the past two weeks, Trump has announced a deal encouraging Russian diesel exports and waived sanctions that were about to be imposed under a law he signed last month. Trump also said on October 19 that he was open to holding a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of an APEC summit next month in China. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it," Trump said. However, he added the main purpose of the meeting would be to discuss "nuclear weapons and denuclearization," rather than Russia's war against Ukraine. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump told reporters when asked whether he would attend a meeting with Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine. Ahead of his visit to Oslo, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive" conversation and a "constructive" discussion with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Zelenskyy said they had discussed several issues, including ballistic missile interceptors, early warning systems for Russian ballistic missile attacks, and the situation regarding Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems. "I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said in a post on X on October 20. SEE ALSO: Rubio Vows To Keep Pushing For Ukraine Peace, Seeks Deeper US Ties In Central Asia Russia continued its attacks on Ukraine, killing at least three people in the Kyiv region and injuring several others. The bodies were discovered as emergency crews battled a fire at a production and storage facility outside the Ukrainian capital, Tymur Tkachenko, the region's military governor, wrote on Telegram . In a separate attack, a Russian drone struck near the Kyiv-Odesa highway, killing three people and injuring four others, according to preliminary reports cited by the Kyiv regional prosecutor's office and regional authorities. The number of casualties was still verified. Overnight, Russian forces attacked three energy facilities in the Odesa region, energy company DTEK reported on October 20, adding that more than 30,000 households remained without electricity following the attack. Meanwhile, Telegram monitoring channels, citing local residents, reported that a diesel fuel storage tank caught fire after Ukrainian drones struck an oil facility in Russia's Tambov region. The Russian military had not immediately confirmed the reported strike but said its air defense forces had intercepted and destroyed 136 Ukrainian drones, including some over the Tambov region. https://www.rferl.org/a/we-re-never-goin.body: Features 'We're Never Going To Be The Major Player': Former Diplomat's Reality Check On US Ambitions In Central Asia By Zamira Eshanova October 19, 2026 14:42 CET 'We're Never Going To Be The Major Player': Former Diplomat's Reality Check On US Ambitions In Central Asia Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Daniel Rosenblum served as deputy assistant secretary of state for Central Asia from 2014 to 2019 before becoming US ambassador to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Speaking in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made clear that business was the focus of his first trip to Central Asia. “We have an incredible delegation, almost 300 Americans that are here with us, and the opportunity to sign billions of dollars of agreements that will both enrich the countries in the region, but also benefit the United States economically," Rubio said on October 19. For Daniel Rosenblum, who served as deputy assistant secretary of state for Central Asia from 2014 to 2019 before becoming US ambassador to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, the scale of the delegation is “unusual.” “I can't think of a precedent where the secretary of state's visit to the region is accompanied by a business mission. We had plenty of business missions in the past. But I don't remember it ever being linked in this way with a secretary's visit. I think it's a good thing and may lead to more successes in terms of deals being signed and new investments,” Rosenblum told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: Rubio Vows To Keep Pushing For Ukraine Peace, Seeks Deeper US Ties In Central Asia But he cautioned against expecting a sudden surge in US investment. High-level attention can open doors, he said, but cannot eliminate the practical obstacles companies face investing in the region. “I would point out that the realities of investing in Central Asia remain the same, regardless of whether the secretary of state is there for the initial contact or not," Rosenblum said. "Some countries are a little bit more welcoming than others. And it's the realities of distance, logistics, financing, finding a good partner. All of those things remain the same, regardless of whether you have 100 companies, 200 companies or 20 companies.” Rubio has said the large business delegation was intended to ensure US companies could compete in markets opening to American commerce. “It's about ensuring that in every part of the world that is opening its doors to American business and American commerce that we're available. That we're showing up and that we're there and that's what this is all about,” Rubio said in Samarkland, adding that major deals would be announced later. While Rosenblum welcomed the focus on commercial ties, the former diplomat was skeptical about a dramatic expansion in US business activity. “I'd be surprised if there's a sudden explosion, where suddenly...10 times as many American companies are doing business as they are today. I think that seems really a stretch to me.” What About Human Rights? The Trump administration’s emphasis on commercial interests marks a departure from the traditional balance of US policy toward Central Asia, Rosenblum said. Previous administrations combined economic and security cooperation with support for democracy, human rights, and market reforms. The current administration, Rosenblum said, has largely dropped the democracy and human rights component from its public agenda. “Some people say -- including some people in Central Asia -- that this is good for the relationship. It's like it makes it easier to talk and to get right to the heart of the matter for business deals or whatever. And I would say it certainly does simplify the relationship," Rosenblum said. "I'm not sure that in the long run, the closeness can be sustained, that is the closeness of our relations with the Central Asian countries, without this [human rights] component,” he said. In Central Asia, power remains concentrated among ruling elites and families, with dynastic succession shaping the political future of several countries. Authoritarian Turkmenistan has already seen power pass from father to son, while similar succession scenarios have emerged in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Kyrgyzstan, once seen by Washington as Central Asia’s democratic exception, has increasingly restricted the political opposition and clamped down on independent media. SEE ALSO: Is Political Opposition Still Possible In Central Asia? Rosenblum said that he thinks democracy and human rights will eventually return to US policy, citing legislation, reporting requirements, and diplomatic tradition. “I believe [human rights will return] because it's in law, in terms of the requirements we have for annual reports on human rights, and various sanctions associated with it. It's in the norms that we've practiced as a country overseas. And it's sort of in our tradition. I believe it's in our DNA. It's in the American DNA," he said. Rosenblum rejected the idea that promoting democracy and protecting US commercial interests are mutually exclusive. “I think that it's possible to promote and extend US interests on security, on business and economic relations, and still also talk about democracy and human rights. It's not either-or, it's not a zero sum [game]," he said. Stronger institutions, he added, can also benefit American companies by creating more predictable conditions for investment. Limits Of US Influence In Central Asia Rubio said Washington was not asking Central Asian countries to “stop talking to somebody else or stop working with other countries,” acknowledging their deep economic ties with powerful neighbors, particularly China. Russia has long maintained significant economic, security, and energy ties across the region. Its war in Ukraine has created new opportunities for Washington, but Rosenblum cautioned against assuming the United States could replace Moscow as the region’s dominant outside power. “I think we can play a role in that, whether it's in the security field, in the economic field, in the international engagement field. The US brings a lot to the table. So, we can be an important player, certainly even more important than we are today. We're never going to be the major player in Central Asia, is my view," Rosenblum said. Rather than seeking dominance, Washington should focus on areas where it has an advantage and where Central Asian governments want US involvement, he said. Rosenblum cited advanced technology, artificial intelligence, and English-language education as fields where US cooperation could help the region diversify its partnerships. He also rejected the idea that China’s growing economic and security presence means the region is already lost to Beijing. “I don't think it's a lost game, if it's even a game,” he said. As Washington uses the C5+1 format -- the main US diplomatic format for engaging Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan -- to expand its engagement, Central Asian governments are navigating a growing number of diplomatic formats with outside powers. “There are more C5 pluses than there are months in the year," Rosenblum said. "So even if you tried to do one a month, you wouldn't be able to get them all in a given year." A longtime advocate of regional integration, Rosenblum said he sees growing cohesion among the five Central Asian countries themselves. “I do believe that the C5 alone, with no pluses or minuses, as I used to say, is developing, is growing, and is incrementally becoming more cohesive,” he said. https://www.rferl.org/a/wider-europe-cro.body: Wider Europe Wider Europe Briefing: Croatia Holds Up Montenegro, Georgia Slips Down EU Agenda October 20, 2026 11:58 CET Wider Europe Briefing: Croatia Holds Up Montenegro, Georgia Slips Down EU Agenda Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Montenegrin Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic (left) and his Croatian counterpart, Gordan Grlic Radman, meet aboard the Jadran sailing ship in Bar, Montenegro's main sea port, in January 2025. Welcome to Wider Europe, RFE/RL's newsletter focusing on the key issues concerning the European Union, NATO, and other institutions and their relationships with the Western Balkans and Europe's Eastern neighborhoods. I'm RFE/RL Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak, and this week I am drilling down on two issues: Croatia’s demands before giving the green light to Montenegro’s EU accession and Georgia’s growing irrelevance in Brussels. Embed share Wider Europe Briefing: Croatia Holds Up Montenegro, Georgia Slips Down EU Agenda by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:12:45 0:00 Direct link 128 kbps | MP3 64 kbps | MP3 Pop-out player Briefing #1: Croatia’s Many Demands On Montenegro Ahead Of Potential EU Membership What You Need To Know: Montenegro’s hopes of finishing its European Union accession talks by the end of the year and joining the club by 2028 have taken a hit after its neighbor and the most recent country to join the bloc, Croatia, presented its final eight demands to Podgorica and fellow EU member states. Croatian officials said that they had communicated them to Montenegro during the summer, and in early October they circulated a paper in Brussels, seen by RFE/RL, titled “Outstanding Issues Between Croatia And Montenegro.” The document states that “certain unexpected unilateral actions by the Montenegrin authorities have rekindled historical tensions and unnecessarily strained bilateral relations, risking the erosion of broad political support for Montenegro’s accession in Croatia.” Not surprisingly, many of the issues hark back to the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s and matters that remain unresolved, with the text stating that “Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of shared history and build a forward-looking relationship with Montenegro. Yet mutual trust and genuine, lasting reconciliation cannot be built without resolving these issues.” Deep Background : During the EU summit in Brussels on October 15-16, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic also fleshed out what Croatia is still demanding from Montenegro before giving its green light to the country’s EU accession. While diplomats from many member states told RFE/RL that they have privately expressed annoyance with Zagreb’s position, which they describe as “unhelpful” and coming at the “eleventh hour” when many are keen to get Montenegro onboard, EU leaders were more understanding of Plenkovic’s position -- perhaps suggesting that enlargement isn’t really the top priority of the union after all. They said that the Croatian leader was “excellent” in communicating what his country wants to see from Montenegro and that he received very little pushback. This was also reflected in the final EU summit conclusions adopted by the European Council, which brings together the bloc’s leaders. The text states that the council “notes the intention of the Irish Council Presidency to work towards the provisional closure of the remaining negotiating chapters, subject to the implementation of the corresponding reforms by Montenegro.” There was no enthusiastic endorsement or warm welcome, with the emphasis instead firmly on Podgorica delivering on its commitments. So far, Montenegro hasn’t reacted publicly to the Croatian demands, making it even harder to gauge how serious the situation is and how long it may take to resolve the outstanding issues. Ireland, which holds the rotating council presidency until the end of the year, is still hoping to close the remaining 12 accession chapters out of the 33 Montenegro needs to become a member, but hardly anyone thinks Dublin will succeed. A Lithuanian diplomat with knowledge of the file thinks that even Vilnius, which takes over the presidency for the first half of 2027, will struggle to get the talks over the line now. Drilling Down So, what exactly is Croatia asking for? Two of the eight demands concern the Morinj camp, where over 300 Croatian nationals were detained between October 1991 and August 1992, following the occupation of part of the Dubrovnik region by Serbian and Montenegrin forces. The first is compensation. The paper states that Zagreb “expects a comprehensive settlement of the issue of compensation for Croatian nationals who were detained and subjected to ill-treatment.” No figure has been mentioned, however. The second demand concerns a memorial plaque at the site. The plaque was jointly unveiled by Croatian and Montenegrin ministers in 2022, but the paper notes that Montenegrin nationalist groups have called for its removal and that “a larger metal frame has since been installed around it, apparently to accommodate a removable panel that could conceal the plaque except during official commemorations.” The third demand also has indirect links to Morinj. It concerns the name of a swimming pool in the Montenegrin city of Kotor that Zagreb wants to change. It is named after Zoran Gopcevic, a former internationally renowned water polo player, who also served as a guard at Morinj. The paper adds that it is “unacceptable for a sports facility to bear the name of an individual associated with the ill-treatment and torture of Croatian detainees.” Another demand involves securing the full “cooperation of the Montenegrin authorities in efforts to establish the fate of 14 Croatian nationals who went missing during the war of aggression against Croatia in the early 1990s” Perhaps the trickiest demand is the fifth, which is closely related to the previous one and concerns the prosecution of war crimes. The document notes that “to date, no convictions have been secured on the basis of command responsibility. In the Morinj case, four members of the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) were convicted of war crimes by final judgments and received sentences totaling twelve years’ imprisonment. However, these convictions did not encompass crimes committed against civilians detained at the camp.” Zagreb is also calling on Podgorica to settle property disputes dating back to the early 1990s involving 51 Croatian families that lived in Montenegro at that time. Then there is perhaps the most publicly prominent dispute -- the potential restitution of the ”Jadran” sailing ship. The three-masted vessel, built in 1933, was historically based in the Croatian coastal city of Split, but when the war broke out, it was in Montenegro, where it has remained ever since. Podgorica maintains that the ship's presence on its territory at the time of Yugoslavia's dissolution gives it legal ownership. Finally, Croatia is also calling for “continued and intensified dialogue on the delimitation of the border between the two countries.” According to the document, this should result in a treaty that “formally confirms that Montenegro has no territorial claims against Croatia.” Interestingly, the maritime border between the two countries also remains unresolved, but the document does not make clear whether settling that dispute is also a condition for Montenegro's EU accession. Instead, it notes that “once the land border issue has been resolved, Croatia would be prepared to convene regular meetings of the expert and intergovernmental commissions responsible for maritime delimitation, without setting specific deadlines.” Briefing #2: Georgia Fading Further From Brussels’ Radar What You Need To Know: If there is one piece of evidence to sh

https://www.rferl.org/a/lavrov-in-tehran.body: Iran Lavrov In Tehran Amid Questions Over Whether Moscow Is Helping Iran In War With US By Kian Sharifi October 19, 2026 15:46 CET Lavrov In Tehran Amid Questions Over Whether Moscow Is Helping Iran In War With US Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrive for a press conference after meeting in Tehran on October 19. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov traveled to Iran on October 19, meeting with President Masud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi amid questions over what support Moscow is providing Tehran to fight its war with the United States. Lavrov traveled to the Iranian capital directly from Manama, Bahrain, where he had attended a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council officials. Gulf states have urged Moscow to use its influence to press Tehran to halt attacks on its neighbors. Following talks in Tehran with his Russian counterpart, Araqchi said they discussed regional and international issues, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Yemen, as well as expanding economic and nuclear cooperation. "Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now," Araqchi wrote in a post on X on October 20. Lavrov also met with Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement, which described the talks in broad terms and provided little detail. The meetings were held in "a traditionally constructive spirit" and with "an emphasis on strengthening the comprehensive strategic partnership," the Russian statement said. It said the "importance of close coordination regarding the situation in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf region, as well as in the South Caucasus and the Caspian region, was underscored, and that Lavrov "reaffirmed Russia’s readiness" to facilitate a resolution to the situation surrounding Iran" -- meaning the war. The Russian statement made no mention of military or intelligence cooperation -- but what was not on the public agenda was the focus of much of the world. After battling a much more powerful adversary for almost eight months, questions about how much support Iran is getting from Russia -- which has never directly entered the war -- and in what form have simmered. SEE ALSO: US Lawmakers, Experts Sound Alarm On Deadly Iran-Russia Axis They came to a boil, however, on October 18 when US President Donald Trump said in a social media post that Russia is doing “very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran” compared to what it could do. That came after he wrote earlier in the week on social media that he did not believe either Moscow nor Beijing were helping Iran “at all.” "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I ⁠don't believe they are ⁠at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote. Trump's October 18 comment was made as part of his justification to waive sweeping sanctions planned against Russia, saying it could drive the Kremlin away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The Trump administration recently waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports, drawing bipartisan condemnation, as well as raising the ire of Ukraine and many of its international partners. 'Russian Support Has Been There' Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFE/RL that while it's true Moscow has withheld heavy weaponry and deals for jets such as the Su-35 fighters have stalled, Russia has still provided Iran with military intelligence enabling “precision strikes against US bases” and helped improve Iranian-made systems, including Shahed drones, through continued military-technical cooperation. “So, it really depends on how you define support, but Russian support has been there, and it has had a tangible impact,” Azizi said. SEE ALSO: From Russia With Expertise: Iranian Students Return Home With Potentially Deadly Knowledge Of Drones, AI, And More Several analysts point to one incident they say shows how important Russia's support for Iran is. In March, Iran attacked the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia that wounded 12 American troops. Experts noted its unusual precision was likely aided by Russian intelligence. Reports then surfaced that two days before the strike, 14 Russian spy satellites passed over the base. Later, US officials concluded that information from Moscow made the precision attack possible. A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak on the record, told RFE/RL that Russian assistance to Iran has always been limited because its war against Ukraine has stretched Moscow’s resources. The official said there was “no sign at all that they are limiting it further” and described Trump's comment as "propaganda to somehow explain to the [US] public why he [is] soft on Russia and bullying Ukraine.” Intelligence, Drones, And Missiles Since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, media reports citing US, European, and Ukrainian officials have described growing Russian support for Tehran. Several media outlets have cited people familiar with US intelligence that Russia has been passing Iran information on the locations and movements of US troops, warships, and aircraft -- much of it satellite imagery. SEE ALSO: If Russia Wants To Stay On Washington's Good Side, Why Help Iran Target US Forces? Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv had evidence that Russia was providing Iran with signals and electronic intelligence. According to Andrea Kendall-Taylor, senior fellow and director of the Transatlantic Security Program at the Center for a New American Security, and Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security, "Russia’s support for Tehran has been operationally meaningful but carefully bounded." "Even as it fights its own war in Ukraine, Moscow has found ways to help Iran strike American targets and sustain the fight through diplomatic cover and material support while stopping short of actions that could draw Russia into direct conflict with the United States," they wrote in an analysis in Foreign Affairs last week. Amir Chahaki, an analyst based in Germany, told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that Putin wants to use Iran as leverage in his dealings with Trump in return for the US applying pressure on Ukraine. “The more Putin can persuade Tehran to move closer to Trump’s demands, the more concessions he can extract from Trump," he said. With reporting by Elaheh Ravanshad of RFE/RL's Radio Farda Lavrov In Tehran Amid Questions Over Whether Moscow Is Helping Iran In War With US Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Kian Sharifi Kian Sharifi is a feature writer specializing in Iranian affairs in RFE/RL's Central Newsroom in Prague. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-space-sat.body: Russia Star Wars: A Russian Military Satellite Gets Very, Very Close To One Used By Ukraine By Mike Eckel October 19, 2026 17:02 CET Updated October 19, 2026 20:30 CET Star Wars: A Russian Military Satellite Gets Very, Very Close To One Used By Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A month after five military satellites were launched from Russia's Plesetsk facility, they were reported maneuvering in ways that would potentially intercept a US-registered, Finnish-operated satellite that provides intelligence to Ukraine. Shortly after midnight on October 18, roughly 1,000 kilometers above the Earth’s surface, a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 did something highly unusual. It moved close to another satellite -- one registered in the United States, operated by a Finnish company, and providing intelligence to Ukraine, among others. How close? By several estimates, 200 meters. Maybe less. "This is provocative. But I view it as typical of the kind of things that Russia does all the time." The incident has grabbed attention -- from amateur satellite watchers and commercial companies, not to mention Western intelligence agencies -- in a way not seen in a long time. It’s also the latest in a series of escalating moves involving not only Russia, but also the United States, China, and other spacefaring, satellite-capable nations, stoking fears of an arms race in space. Or worse: a space war. "This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, said on October 19. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations." “What is new is that I don't think that there has ever been a close approach that was uncoordinated” between these two exact satellites, said Victoria Samson, a space analyst at the Secure World Foundation, a Washington think tank. “Russia could be doing this close approach to interfere with” the Finnish satellite’s “broadcasting, to jam it, or to listen to what it's listening to, or to intimidate it, or even possibly to physically harm it,” she said. SEE ALSO: Debris Clouds, Endangered Astronauts: What The Fallout From A Russian Anti-Satellite Test Means For Space “I’d say it is being viewed as concerning and aggressive with potential hostile intent,” said Douglas Loverro, a former top space policy official at NASA and the US Defense Department, “but I also think cooler heads believe it is signaling on the part of the Russians. Meanwhile, I think the Russians are schooling us on our behavior.” “If accurate, 150 meters is an exceptionally close approach and is unlikely to be operationally routine,” said Bruce McClintock, a retired Air Force brigadier general who is now a space policy researcher at the RAND Corporation. That “is a legitimate safety and security concern, but it should not automatically be described as an attack or proof of hostile intent.” Past Trajectories During the Cold War space race, both Moscow and Washington deployed weapons in orbit, testing and detonating nuclear devices, some of which wreaked havoc on satellite communications. The tit-for-tat detonations paved the way for the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which permanently banned deploying atomic weapons in space. The treaty did not preclude anti-satellite warfare, building and deploying technologies to disrupt or destroy another countries’ orbiting devices. The countries conducted at least 50 anti-satellite tests during the Cold War, according to the Secure World Foundation. SEE ALSO: Russia's Security Agency Pulls Ambitious Satellite Internet Venture Back To Earth In the 1980s, the US military tested jet-launched missiles that would target orbiting satellites. But the result was clouds of shrapnel that catapulted around the planet at potentially lethal speeds. Congress canceled the program. In 2007, China used a ground-launched missile to destroy an aging weather satellite at an altitude of around 865 kilometers. According to the Union of Concerned Scientists, the event "created more persistent debris than any other event in space." "This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by'." A year later, the US military used its sea-based Aegis missile-defense system to destroy a nonoperational satellite. In that case, the satellite destruction occurred at a lower altitude, and the debris that was sprayed out only lasted in orbit for a short time. In 2019, India surprised the global space community by conducting its own anti-satellite test. That object was destroyed at around 282 kilometers above the Earth, in a way that experts said minimized the longevity or breadth of an orbiting debris cloud. In December 2020, Russia tested a missile that destroyed a defunct military satellite -- and resulted in a debris cloud that later endangered the International Space Station. US officials say Russia also appears to have tested “nesting doll” satellites: objects designed to house smaller satellites that are then launched while in orbit. This past April, Russia sent six satellites from its northern Plesetsk launch facility into a low Earth orbit. The Plesetsk cosmodrome, located in Russia's far north, is an important launch facility for Russia's military satellites. A month later, according to the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, five of them maneuvered in a way that gave them the potential to intercept another object: a nonmilitary, commercial satellite operated by ICEYE, a Finnish company that provides “space-based intelligence to Ukraine.” That satellite, dubbed ICEYE-X36, includes synthetic aperture radar , a technology that allows for more detailed ground imagery and can be used day or night, even in cloudy conditions. In a statement released in May, US Space Force said the Russian satellites were positioned close to a "Western commercial radar satellite used by Ukraine for imagery intelligence,” but did not identify it. In a statement to RFE/RL on October 19, ICEYE, which is based in Espoo, Finland, said: “We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely." Late last week, one of the Russian military satellites, Kosmos-2612, began positioning itself closer to ICEYE-X36, according to satellite trackers . Then, over the weekend, Kosmos-2612 moved even closer. Very close. Major General Michael Traut, the head of Germany’s space command, described the Russian spacecraft as “chasing” the ICEYE satellite . “It is reasonable to regard an unannounced close approach as concerning and potentially escalatory,” McClintock said, “but proximity alone does not establish hostile intent or an imminent attack.” SEE ALSO: NASA Rebukes Russian Space Agency After Cosmonauts Display Occupied Ukrainian Flags "While the intention behind Kosmos-2612's behavior remains uncertain, the deliberate nature of the activity, the fuel required to conduct this activity, and the proximity to a Western commercial imaging satellite make the event strategically important," LeoLabs said. 'This Is Provocative' Last month, the United States caused a jolt with its own unexpected announcement: Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” the secretary of the US Air Force told a conference outside of Washington. For longtime space watchers, that announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time. “The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities,” wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department . “An arms race in space has been under way for years.” Depending on what happens next with Kosmos-2612 -- if something does happen to the Finnish-operated satellite -- there could be grounds for a formal complaint under the Outer Space Treaty. https://dushanbe.osce.org/news/programme.body: News News Item OSCE fosters collaboration on Tajikistan’s Green Economy Strategy through national roundtable Issued on: 19 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Environmental activities The OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, in co-operation with the Ministry of Economic Development and Trade of the Republic of Tajikistan (MEDT), organized a national roundtable on “Green Economy Development in the Republic of Tajikistan” to advance dialogue on implementing the country’s Green Economy Development Strategy for 2023-2037. The roundtable fostered collaboration among government institutions, the private sector, academia and environmental stakeholders, enabling them to share progress, address implementation challenges and identify opportunities to advance Tajikistan’s green economy transition. Presentations during the roundtable covered a broad range of topics. MEDT presented progress in implementing the Strategy and the national Taxonomy, while the OSCE outlined its joint activities in support of the country’s green economy agenda. The National Bank of Tajikistan spoke on the development of green financing in the banking system, while LLC “Green Technologies,” a private company, gave a presentation on how the quality of technology shapes the economics of solar energy projects. The International University of Tourism and Entrepreneurship explored the links between climate change, labour markets and food security in the context of the Sustainable Development Goals. The Dushanbe Aarhus Centre, operating under the Committee for Environmental Protection, highlighted the role of Aarhus Centres in supporting the transition to a green economy. By facilitating exchanges across sectors, the roundtable helped connect policy priorities with practical considerations, including access to green finance, renewable energy technologies and the social and economic implications of climate change. The discussions also highlighted areas where continued co-operation among national institutions and international partners can support implementation of the Strategy and its Action Plan. The event forms part of the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe’s efforts to support Tajikistan in implementing environmental legislation and policies, promoting co-operation and advancing sustainable, resource-efficient development Contacts Anisa Hojieva National Communications and Outreach Officer OSCE Program Office in Dushanbe 18 A A.Donish street Dushanbe Tajikistan Email: anisa.hojieva@osce.org Munira Shoinbekova Senior Press and Public Information Assistant OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe 18a Ahmadi Donish Avenue 734012 Dushanbe Tajikistan Email: Munira.Shoinbekova@osce.org Phone: +992 37 2265014 /15 /16 /17 /18 Fax: +992 37 2265019 Contact OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe 18a Ahmadi Donish Avenue 734012 Dushanbe Tajikistan Phone: +992 37 2265014/15/16/17/18 Email: POiD@osce.org Social media: @OSCETajikistan @OSCEDushanbe @oscedushanbe

https://bishkek.osce.org/news/programme-.body: News News Item OSCE strengthens inter-agency co-operation to protect victims of human trafficking in Kyrgyzstan Issued on: 20 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyz Republic, 16 October 2026 From 12 to 16 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek, in co-operation with the Ministry of Labour, Social Security and Migration of the Kyrgyz Republic and the State Customs Service under the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic, organized a National Simulation Exercise on strengthening inter-agency co-operation and social protection systems for victims of human trafficking at Issyk-Kul. The exercise provided a practical platform for participants to simulate complex scenarios, test their decision-making and learn from mistakes in a safe and controlled environment. Such exercises are essential for preparing relevant professionals to respond effectively to real-life situations, where timely and well-coordinated action can be critical to the safety, well-being and future of victims of human trafficking. Beyond developing practical skills, the exercise aimed to strengthen co-operation among relevant institutions and foster a co-ordinated, victim-centred approach to identifying potential victims of human trafficking and ensuring they receive appropriate protection, assistance and support. By bringing together relevant stakeholders to practise joint responses, the simulation exercise contributed to strengthening national capacities to identify and protect victims of human trafficking and improve co-ordination among the institutions responsible for their safety and social reintegration. https://omik.osce.org/news/mission-kosov.body: News News Item Young women from Prishtinë/Priština and Belgrade explore dialogue and shared futures at OSCE Academy Issued on: 17 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission in Kosovo Fields of work: Gender equality , Youth The 12th edition of the OSCE Dialogue Academy for Young Women, organized by the OSCE Mission in Kosovo in co-operation with the OSCE Mission to Serbia, concluded on 17 October in the cross-border cities of Nova Gorica, Slovenia, and Gorizia, Italy. Held on 8-17 October, the programme brought together 23 young women from Prishtinë/Priština and Belgrade, representing diverse professional and community backgrounds. This year's edition took place in Nova Gorica and Gorizia, joint European Capitals of Culture for 2025, providing a relevant setting for exploring dialogue, reconciliation, difficult histories and shared futures. The programme combined interactive training, dialogue circles, practical exercises and exchanges with guest speakers, strengthening participants’ skills in communication, negotiation, mediation and conflict transformation, while exploring identities, historical narratives, women's leadership and peacebuilding. Participants met with the Heads of the OSCE Missions, Ambassador Gerard McGurk and Ambassador Marcel Peško; Irish Ambassador Ragnar Almqvist and Caroline Phelan; and renowned peace activist Bronagh Hinds, whose experience in the Northern Ireland peace process offered insights into women's leadership, inclusive peacebuilding and the importance of sustained dialogue. A World Café discussion brought participants together with local cultural and civil society representatives, including Stojan Pelko, Director of the Slovenian Cinematheque; Daniela Klanjšček of the Lojze Bratuž Cultural Centre; and Mateja Jančar of the Women Writers Route. Discussions explored the cultural, historical and societal dimensions of the Nova Gorica-Gorizia region, including the role of film, cultural heritage and cross-border initiatives. Through the established partnership with the European Grouping of Territorial Cooperation GO (EGTC GO), participants also learned about efforts to develop shared cultural initiatives and cross-border co-operation in a historically divided region, as well as how co-operation can help communities address divisions and build shared futures. Following the Academy, participants will have the opportunity to join the Dialogue Academy Network of Alumnae (DANA), a growing network of more than 270 young women committed to advancing dialogue, mutual understanding and co-operation. Through DANA, alumnae continue to participate in joint initiatives, exchanges and capacity-building activities, maintaining connections beyond the Academy itself. Organized annually since 2015 under the auspices of the Follow Us Initiative, the Dialogue Academy reflects the joint commitment of the OSCE Mission in Kosovo and the OSCE Mission to Serbia to strengthening young women's participation in dialogue, conflict resolution, peacebuilding and decision-making processes. Contacts Maid Konjhodžić Head of Office of Political Affairs and Communications OSCE Mission in Kosovo 12 Abdyl Frashëri 10000 Prishtinë/Priština Kosovo Email: Maid.Konjhodzic@osce.org Phone: +383 38 240 100 1191 +383 49 957 600 Edita Buçaj National Deputy Spokesperson OSCE Mission in Kosovo 12 Abdyl Frashëri 10000 Prishtinë/Priština Kosovo Email: Edita.Bucaj@osce.org Phone: +383 49 950 163 +383 38 240100 1118 Contact OSCE Mission in Kosovo 12 Abdyl Frashëri 10000 Prishtinë/Priština Kosovo Phone: +383 49 957 600 Email: Maid.Konjhodzic@osce.org Social media: @oscekosovo @oscekosovo @oscekosovo @oscekosovo
