https://24.kg/en/article/292-citizens-co.body: During the first nine months of 2026, 292 individuals who had been convicted and were serving sentences abroad were transferred to Kyrgyzstan. Deputy Prosecutor General Umutkan Konkubaeva said during a meeting of the Zhogorku Kenesh Committee on International Affairs, Defense, Security, and Migration. According to her, the number of citizens being transferred back to their home country to continue serving their sentences is increasing year by year. In 2021, 66 individuals were transferred to the Kyrgyz Republic; in 2022, there were 54; in 2023 — 79; in 2024 — 128; and in 2025 — 237. Member of Parliament Zhanybek Amatov noted that parliamentarians are frequently approached regarding this issue and requested an explanation of the procedure for transferring convicted persons. Umutkan Konkubaeva explained that Kyrgyzstan has entered into international agreements with a number of states. These agreements allow citizens convicted abroad to continue serving their sentences in their home country. She stated that the relatives of a convicted person may contact the Prosecutor General’s Office to initiate the process. The office then submits a request to the foreign state. Furthermore, the convicted individual must provide written consent for the transfer. «There are no additional costs for the citizens involved. There is no need to hire a lawyer. All expenses related to the transfer are covered by the state, in accordance with international agreements,» the Deputy Prosecutor General emphasized.

https://24.kg/article/v-kyrgyzstan-za-de.body: За девять месяцев 2026 года в Кыргызстан перевели 292 человека, осужденных за рубежом и отбывающих наказание. Об этом сообщила заместитель генерального прокурора Умуткан Конкубаева на заседании комитета Жогорку Кенеша по международным делам, обороне, безопасности и миграции. По ее словам, число граждан, которых переводят на родину для дальнейшего отбывания наказания, растет из года в год. В 2021 году в КР перевели 66 человек, в 2022-м — 54, в 2023-м — 79, в 2024-м — 128, а в 2025-м — 237. Депутат Жаныбек Аматов отметил, что к парламентариям часто обращаются по этому вопросу, и попросил разъяснить процедуру перевода осужденных. Умуткан Конкубаева пояснила, что между Кыргызстаном и рядом государств заключены международные соглашения. Благодаря им граждане, осужденные за рубежом, могут продолжить отбывать наказание на родине. По ее словам, для этого родственники осужденного могут обратиться в Генеральную прокуратуру. Ведомство направляет запрос в иностранное государство. При этом осужденный должен письменно согласиться на перевод. «Дополнительных расходов для граждан не требуется. Нанимать адвоката не надо. Все расходы на перевод покрывает государство в соответствии с международными соглашениями», — подчеркнула заместитель генпрокурора.

https://24.kg/article/polovina-osuzhdenn.body: В зарубежных тюрьмах находятся 1 тысяча 319 граждан Кыргызстана, осужденных за различные преступления. Об этом на заседании комитета ЖК по судебно-правовым вопросам, правопорядку, борьбе с преступностью и противодействию коррупции сообщила заместитель генерального прокурора Умуткан Конкубаева. По ее словам, статистику по осужденным за рубежом ведет Министерство иностранных дел. Согласно данным ведомства, большинство кыргызстанцев отбывают наказание в России — 1 тысяча 3 человека. В Казахстане находятся 109 осужденных граждан, в Узбекистане — 55, в Ираке — 41. Умуткан Конкубаева отметила, что многие осужденные за рубежом не хотят возвращаться на родину для дальнейшего отбывания наказания. Даже если их родственники подают соответствующее заявление, перевод невозможен без согласия самого осужденного. По ее словам, одна из причин отказа заключается в том, что судимость, полученная за рубежом, не считается судимостью в Кыргызстане. «В последнее время число желающих вернуться увеличивается. Это связано с ситуацией в России», — сказала она. Депутаты также поинтересовались случаями, когда в РФ осужденные соглашаются отправиться на войну, чтобы избежать дальнейшего отбывания наказания в тюрьме. Умуткан Конкубаева сообщила, что в прокуратуру поступали обращения по этому вопросу. Однако при проверке совместно с российской стороной выяснялось, что у некоторых осужденных есть российское гражданство. В таких случаях кыргызстанские правоохранительные органы не могут вмешиваться во внутренние дела другого государства. При этом, по словам замгенпрокурора, Кыргызстан не возвращает для отбывания наказания на родине граждан, осужденных за особо тяжкие преступления, в том числе терроризм и экстремизм. С начала года в Кыргызстан для дальнейшего отбывания наказания перевели 292 человека, осужденных за рубежом.

https://24.kg/article/konstruktory-pod-z.body: В Кыргызстане предлагают продлить запрет на ввоз кузовов легковых автомобилей еще на шесть месяцев. Соответствующий проект постановления кабинета министров вынесен на общественное обсуждение. Власти объясняют необходимость ограничений борьбой с незаконной сборкой машин, известной как «конструкторы». Как отмечается в справке-обосновании, такие авто собирают из отдельно ввезенных кузовов, двигателей и других агрегатов. При этом, по данным разработчиков документа, некоторые автомобили не проходят надлежащее таможенное оформление, а для их регистрации используются поддельные документы. Отдельной проблемой названа замена кузовов уже зарегистрированных машин. Власти считают, что таким способом могут легализовываться авто, ввезенные без уплаты таможенных пошлин и налогов. По данным Кыргызского центра аккредитации, в рамках легализации автомобилей на технический осмотр направили 30 тысяч 730 единиц. Из них 466 не прошли проверку, поскольку собраны из разных авто либо не соответствовали техническим требованиям. Еще 30 тысяч 264 машины успешно прошли техосмотр, однако государственную регистрацию завершили 30 тысяч 86. Оставшиеся 178 автомобилей процедуру легализации не закончили. Общая расчетная сумма легализационных платежей составила 1 миллиард 811 миллионов 850 тысяч сомов. Кроме того, среди легализованных авто оказались 944 машины, ранее задержанные сотрудниками ГКНБ и помещенные на штрафстоянки. Проект предусматривает запрет на ввоз автомобильных кузовов категории M1 на шесть месяцев. При этом ограничения не будут распространяться на таможенный транзит и кузова, предназначенные для производства и сборки автомобилей восемью указанными в документе предприятиями. В перечень исключений вошли компании «ДТ Техник», «Шумкар», «Жису», «Шунфа», «Мурат Авто», «Кыргыз Унаа Курулуш», «Меридиан Голд» и «Белес Групп КейЖи». Как следует из справки-обоснования, часть предприятий уже занимается сборкой автомобилей, остальные находятся на стадии строительства производственных мощностей. Разработчики считают, что продление запрета позволит сократить теневой оборот машин, предотвратить уклонение от таможенных платежей и повысить безопасность дорожного движения. Напомним, аналогичные ограничения вводились ранее. Новым постановлением предлагается признать утратившим силу решение кабинета министров от 20 мая 2026 года No 357. В случае принятия постановление вступит в силу через 10 дней после официального опубликования, а сам запрет начнет действовать еще через три дня.

https://www.azernews.az/region/265862.ht.body: South Korea reduces diplomatic presence in Ukraine over POW dispute 20 October 2026 12:08 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more South Korea has withdrawn additional staff from its embassy in Ukraine amid a dispute over North Korean prisoners of war, Yonhap reported. The South Korean Foreign Ministry said the decision was made because it had not received a constructive response from the Ukrainian side regarding the North Korean POW issue. The move comes several weeks after Seoul recalled its ambassador to Ukraine over the same situation. The dispute between Ukraine and South Korea emerged following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s address to the UN General Assembly on September 23. At the time, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had handed over to Seoul two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces in the Kursk region in January 2025. It was noted that South Korea had expected the information about the transfer to remain confidential. President Lee Jae-myung accused Ukraine of disclosing the information and said that the confidentiality was intended to protect the prisoners and their families, who remain in North Korea. On October 7, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said the disagreement with South Korea stemmed from differing interpretations of confidentiality arrangements concerning the transfer of the two North Korean prisoners of war. According to Tykhyi, the two sides had agreed in advance on the details of the transfer and began holding private negotiations through closed channels after the dispute emerged. https://tass.com/world/2204425.body: Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after meeting Zelensky in Oslo — Axios reporter US Presidential Special Envoy intends to discuss with Russian President Vladimir Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff © Evelyn Hockstein/Pool Photo via AP WASHINGTON, October 20. /TASS/. US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff hopes to visit Russia and meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin after holding talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, Barak Ravid, a correspondent for Axios and Israel’s Channel 12, said on X, citing sources. According to the sources, Witkoff is currently flying to Oslo for a meeting with Zelensky scheduled for Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, France, the European Union leadership, and NATO, are expected to take part in the talks. "The objective is to continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia," Ravid said. According to one of his sources, Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after Oslo, where he intends to discuss with Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners. Last week, representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe worked on developing these proposals at the technical level. They include the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old US citizen convicted in Russia of fighting on the side of the Ukrainian armed forces. "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia", a US official told Ravid, adding. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump’s objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States." Jared Kushner, a special envoy and son-in-law of the US president, will not accompany Witkoff in person this time because he has the flu. He will participate in the consultations remotely. On October 1, Putin said Russia would like to end hostilities in Ukraine through a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Moscow is ready for negotiations but sees no willingness on the part of the Kiev government to engage in talks, the president added. https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/10/20/health.body: Photo: AP The ministry’s press service issued the clarification in response to reports that 290 suspected measles cases had been recorded in Tashkent and more than 10,000 people who had been in contact with patients had been identified. The figures circulating on social media cover the cumulative total for the first nine months of 2026, rather than cases identified over a short period or the current situation, the ministry said. “Currently, the epidemiological situation regarding measles in Tashkent and throughout the country is stable. There is no reason for concern,” the statement said. The Committee for Sanitary and Epidemiological Welfare and Public Health urged social media users not to misinterpret the figures. The ministry also provided vaccination data for the capital. During the first nine months of 2026, 47,494 one-year-old children and 42,767 six-year-old children in Tashkent received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine as part of the routine immunization program.

https://www.trend.az/casia/kazakhstan/42.body: Home Central Asia Kazakhstan Tokayev appoints new head of Kazakhstan's presidential communications department Kazakhstan News 20 October 2026 14:29 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Aqorda Alyona Pavlenko Journalist, International Desk Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Yevgeniy Kochetov has been appointed head of the Communications Department of the Presidential Administration of Kazakhstan, according to an order issued by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Under another order, Askar Umarov has been relieved of his post as director of the Central Communications Service under the President of Kazakhstan. Kanat Kulshmanov has been appointed director of the Central Communications Service under the President of Kazakhstan and relieved of his previous position, according to the orders. According to Kazakhstan's Paragraph information system, Kochetov has served as vice minister of culture and information since November 2023. He previously served as vice minister of information and social development from February to August 2023. His previous positions also include director of the Central Communications Service at the Ministry of Information and Communications from October 2016 to May 2017, chairman of the board of Kazcontent from May 2017 to September 2018, and director general of the Media Damytu Qory corporate foundation from 2020 to April 2022. Kochetov also worked as a journalist and economic columnist for several publications, including Liter, Kapital, Vlast and Informburo, and held management positions in the private sector. Meanwhile, Kulshmanov was born on September 5, 1987, in Kazakhstan's Kostanay Region. He began his career in 2007 as a correspondent in the political and legal information sector of the Kazinform national news agency. From 2012 to 2016, he worked as a journalist for Kazcontent. Kulshmanov subsequently held positions in media monitoring and analysis at the Ministry of National Economy, served as press secretary to the akim of Aktobe Region from 2017 to 2019, and worked as press secretary and director of the public relations department at the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of the Population from 2019 to 2020. From 2020 to 2021, he served as deputy head of the office of the akim of Zhambyl Region, followed by a position as head of the press service of KazMunayGas from 2021 to 2022. From 2022 to 2024, Kulshmanov was press secretary to the Prime Minister of Kazakhstan. In 2024-2025, he served as deputy head of the Communications Department of the Presidential Administration. On March 11, 2025, Kulshmanov was appointed head of the Communications Department of the Presidential Administration. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4236355..body: Home Azerbaijan Chronicles of Victory: President Ilham Aliyev addresses Azerbaijani people on liberation of Zangilan on October 20, 2020 (PHOTO/VIDEO) Azerbaijan News 20 October 2026 07:00 (UTC +04:00) BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline. The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has addressed the nation. Trend presents the address. Nationwide address of President Ilham Aliyev - Dear fellow compatriots. The victorious Azerbaijani Army is gaining new victories on the battlefield. These victories make every Azerbaijani citizen happy. The enemy, which has been occupying our lands for almost 30 years, sees the strength of the Azerbaijani Army on the battlefield. We are fighting on our own land, defending our own land, and we will continue to drive the invaders out of our lands. Our people are looking forward to more news from the battlefield and the frontline. I am very happy. I am a very lucky person to be able to convey this good news to the people of Azerbaijan. The liberation of every village, every city and every strategic height from the occupiers requires great professionalism, courage, bravery and heroism. Our servicemen are becoming martyrs. May Allah rest the souls of all our martyrs in peace! Our martyrs will always live in our hearts. Our servicemen are getting wounded on the battlefield. May Allah send healing to all our wounded soldiers! At the same time, the hated enemy is constantly firing on our settlements. Every day, our cities and villages along the frontline come under fire from the hated enemy. Tartar district is particularly exposed to cowardly fire. At the same time, the enemy fires on Aghdam, Goranboy, Aghjabadi, Barda, other cities and districts. As a result of the cowardly shelling of the city of Ganja, civilians were killed – children, women, the elderly. But it does not matter to the enemy. There is no difference for them. They are defeated on the battlefield, they are unable to stand in front of the Azerbaijani Army and commit crimes against the civilian population in front of the whole world in order to stop us and strike at us. The whole world sees what an ugly and savage enemy Azerbaijan is liberating its native lands from. For 30 years, they sat on our lands and tried to challenge us. For 30 years, they exploited our lands, exploited our natural resources. Theft and looting are their trademarks. Suffice it to look at the destroyed villages and cities to see what savages we are facing. There is not a single safe building in the occupied and already liberated lands. All buildings have been demolished and looted. Our historical sites, mosques and graves have been destroyed, looted and desecrated. They thought that the Azerbaijani people would put up with this situation. They thought that these lands would be occupied forever. They changed the names of our cities, changed the borders of our districts, changed the names of our villages, wanted to Armenianize our lands but could not achieve this. They could not break the will of the Azerbaijani people. Every Azerbaijani who has not seen their native lands, who opened their eyes to the world after the occupation lived with a desire to return to these lands. We saw it in the example of Jojug Marjanly. Young people born after the occupation, each of them cherished the dream of returning to Jojug Marjanly. I am sure that the citizens of Azerbaijan will return to all the lands liberated from the occupiers. They will live in those lands again and build there in peace and tranquility – just as the cultural heritage of the Azerbaijani people has been created in all the once occupied lands. But the hated enemy wanted to destroy this heritage, destroyed our mosques. When we built a mosque similar to the Shusha mosque in the village of Jojug Marjanly and opened it, I said that they may have destroyed the buildings of mosques but these mosques live in our hearts, and one day all our destroyed mosques will be restored, all our cities and villages will be restored. We are on the threshold of the Great Return, and the Azerbaijani state will do its best to ensure that citizens of Azerbaijan return to the occupied and liberated lands and live there in peace and tranquility. Life will be revived in these lands. Our IDPs have lived all these years with a dream although many of them have wonderful conditions. As you know, this year alone we plan to provide 7,000 apartments to the IDPs. More than 300,000 IDPs have been provided with houses and apartments. They are grateful to us for this care, they have expressed their gratitude in our numerous meetings. But at the same time, I knew myself and they asked me to return them to their land. They understood that this was a difficult issue, they were perfectly aware that this required certain geopolitical conditions. They believed in me, and I told them that we would return them to those lands. I told them that I knew what to do, when and how. The trust people placed in me allowed us the opportunity to resolve this issue. I declare again that I keep all the promises I make. I am true to all the promises I make. The main goal of my activity as President is the return of Azerbaijani lands, the restoration of territorial integrity, and we are doing it on the battlefield today. The negotiations did not yield any results for almost 30 years. The fortifications Armenia built in the occupied territories show that they did not intend to give up these lands. They simply deceived us and international mediators. They were simply biding time, while at the same time conducting illegal settlement of the occupied territories. They settled thousands of people in the city of Lachin, thousands more in Kalbajar. They lived in our villages we have liberated today – in Fuzuli, Jabrayil and other districts. Most of those villages are destroyed, but in some houses they lived on our lands. Having carried out ethnic cleansing against the Azerbaijanis, having committed genocide against the Azerbaijanis and having expelled our citizens from their native lands, they held a "referendum", which is completely contrary to human morality, laws and international law. No-one recognizes the so-called "Nagorno-Karabakh republic". Now they are trying to get countries of the world to recognize the so-called criminal entity. They have lost their mind. They do not understand that no-one will do it. They do not understand that every country that does this can no longer be considered a friendly country for Azerbaijan. Not only that, we will cut all ties with such a country. They lost their mind. They are trying to restore the status quo now. I have said there is no status quo. We have destroyed the status quo and we have done what is right. We have been waiting for about 30 years. Ten years ago, at the level of the Minsk Group co-chairs and their presidents, a statement was made that the status quo was unacceptable. We also supported it, we liked it, we had high hopes, and then some progress at the negotiating table raised our hopes. But the hated enemy simply deceived us and the international community. This is disrespect for international mediators. We changed the status quo by showing strength on the battlefield. I said this before these clashes, I have said this several times. Unfortunately, international law does not work in international relations. If it did, four UN Security Council resolutions would have been implemented long ago. We waited for 20 years for these resolutions to be implemented. They simply remained on paper. Why? Because there was no political will, there was no mechanism for the implementation

https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202610/2.body: Iran warns of retaliation as Trump backs Netanyahu - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Middle East Home / World / Middle East Iran warns of retaliation as Trump backs Netanyahu By CUI HAIPEI in Dubai, UAE, and JAN YUMUL in Hong Kong | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-20 09:21 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE People search the rubble for survivors in Yemen's Saada Province on Sunday after an airstrike reportedly carried out by Saudi Arabia. At least nine people were killed in the attack, according to al-Masirah, a Houthi-run television channel. XINHUA Iran has threatened retaliation if its energy infrastructure is attacked again, while US President Donald Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of a tightly contested election. Tehran, meanwhile, said its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remains on the table, even as its military reported that a supertanker had hit a naval mine while using an unauthorized route. It was the latest such incident since Iran tightened its control of the key waterway after war erupted on Feb 28 following US and Israeli strikes on Iranian territory. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Monday that the tanker had taken the strait's "unauthorized southern route" and disabled its positioning and navigation systems. The Fars News Agency quoted the IRGC as saying the vessel "exploded and caught fire in its engine room after hitting a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz". The incident came after Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, bolstering the veteran leader's bid for another term. "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote on Truth Social, using Netanyahu's nickname. Netanyahu said in a video later that his close ties with Trump could help "eliminate the Iranian threat" if he wins the election. In response, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused Netanyahu of "driving America into another war to stay out of jail". "Last time you wanted to 'finish the job', Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful: We have unfinished jobs too," he wrote on X. Araghchi said Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within six days and resume negotiations with the United States on the seventh remains on the table. Amid the escalating conflict, the US issued security alerts across 12 Middle Eastern countries on Sunday, warning of potential threats from Iran or Yemen's Houthi militia and possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions. The countries included Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Iran, Lebanon, Yemen and Israel. Following an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people on Oct 10, Egypt said on Sunday it was ready to support Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its security and stability. Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government and the Houthis, who control Sanaa and much of the north, has opened another front amid the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran. At least 53 soldiers were killed and more than 200 were injured on Monday when three missiles struck the al-Alam military camp in Yemen's Shabwa Province, provincial authorities said. The Houthis have acknowledged targeting the camp. Al-Alam is a large military facility in Jardan district used by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government and supported by the Saudi Arabia-led coalition. Agencies contributed to this story. https://www.rferl.org/a/rubio-ukraine-pe.body: News Rubio Vows To Keep Pushing For Ukraine Peace, Seeks Deeper US Ties In Central Asia By Alex Raufoglu October 19, 2026 11:29 CET Rubio Vows To Keep Pushing For Ukraine Peace, Seeks Deeper US Ties In Central Asia Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (right) meets with Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on October 19. SAMARKAND -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would continue efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, warning that the conflict risks escalating beyond the two countries as he met with Central Asian officials in Uzbekistan. Speaking to reporters in Samarkand on October 19, Rubio defended President Donald Trump's push for negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv, acknowledged limited progress, and said Washington remained open to any opportunity to secure a settlement. “No one's winning that war,” Rubio said. “People are dying every day. Things are being blown up every day. Things are being destroyed every day.” Rubio's visit, which brought nearly 300 American business representatives to Uzbekistan, also highlighted Washington's efforts to expand economic ties with Central Asia, a region where China has become the leading trading partner while Russia retains longstanding security and economic links. SEE ALSO: Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China Meeting with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan under the C5+1 framework, Rubio said the US wanted to strengthen its presence without demanding that regional governments choose between competing powers. Asked about reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin had proposed a meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war, Rubio said discussions about a possible meeting had taken place but that he did not believe all arrangements had been finalized. Trump remained committed to ending the conflict, Rubio said, adding that Washington would continue testing opportunities for negotiations despite the lack of progress so far. “This is not a criminal case,” Rubio said when asked what evidence the administration had that Putin was serious about peace talks. “This is about diplomacy, and in diplomacy, you continue to try.” He said a deal would ultimately depend on whether both sides were willing to make concessions. Rubio: Dangers Beyond Ukraine Rubio also defended the administration's decision to suspend certain sanctions for 60 days, saying it was intended to give ongoing talks with Russia and Ukraine a chance to produce results. He cited the war's mounting human and economic costs, referring to Trump's repeated claim that as many as 25,000 people are dying each month in the fighting. Rubio warned that the conflict posed dangers beyond Ukraine and Russia, particularly for Eastern Europe. Drones disrupted by electronic warfare, failed sabotage operations, and other incidents could cause damage in neighboring countries and risk triggering a wider confrontation, he said. The US wanted to bring the war to an end because of both its devastating consequences and the risk of escalation, Rubio added. SEE ALSO: Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders Asked about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's assertion that Washington had temporarily paused some intelligence sharing with Kyiv before resuming it, Rubio said there had been no interruption. “I don't know where he's getting these things from or why he's saying these things to the press,” Rubio said. He also declined to comment on reports that Ukraine had not received advance warning before Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, saying he did not know the details of that incident. He acknowledged that US officials had examined a software problem involving Ukraine's early-warning system in an earlier episode. Rubio said Washington had not changed its diplomatic presence in Kyiv, although the safety of US diplomats and facilities remained a concern. Asked whether relations between the Trump and Zelenskyy administrations had fundamentally broken down, Rubio said Washington's priority was to end the war. He acknowledged that Ukraine wanted to expand its use of the Starshield satellite communications system, which is controlled by the US Department of War, to conduct attacks beyond Ukrainian territory. He declined to discuss those negotiations further. US Seeks To Compete With China Rubio's visit also underscored Washington's ambition to gain a stronger economic foothold in Central Asia, where China is the principal trading partner of all five countries. Chinese companies have secured deals involving regional energy resources and minerals, while Russia remains connected to the region through pipelines, security arrangements, and labor migration. Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has encouraged Central Asian governments to diversify their international relationships. Asked how the US intended to compete with China, Rubio said Washington was seeking a fair opportunity for American businesses rather than asking regional governments to sever existing ties. “This is not about coming here to say stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country,” he said. Rubio said the US delegation had come to identify investment and trade opportunities, with agreements worth billions of dollars expected to be announced. Uzbekistan, he added, wanted to maintain relationships with multiple powers. “They want to be friends to everybody,” Rubio said of the Uzbek government. “They want to have a relationship with everybody.” SEE ALSO: As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere He described Uzbekistan as a key regional player, citing its population, economic development, and tourism potential. Rubio said the country's reported annual economic growth of nearly 8 percent offered significant opportunities for further cooperation. He also called for greater US engagement with Central Asia, saying the region had not received the attention it deserved from American policymakers over the past two decades. The visit was intended to establish a foundation for longer-term cooperation, Rubio said, rather than simply produce a series of immediate commercial agreements. Critical Minerals And Energy Security Rubio also highlighted the importance of diversifying global supply chains, particularly for critical minerals used in advanced technologies and industries. “It's just not smart for the whole world to depend on one place for 100 percent of anything,” he said, arguing that excessive dependence on a single supplier left countries vulnerable to political tensions and disruptions. Countries with critical minerals and the ability to process them, he said, had an economic interest in developing those resources responsibly. Washington was interested in partnerships that could benefit local economies while diversifying supplies for American and global industries. SEE ALSO: Trump Defends Russia Sanctions Waivers, Zelenskyy Says Kyiv Attacked Without Early Warning From Partners On energy, Rubio defended the administration's use of sanctions waivers affecting Russian oil supplies, rejecting the suggestion that the measures meant Washington had changed its position on purchases of Russian energy. He said decisions had to take into account global prices, energy availability, and the economic circumstances of individual countries, including their ability to find alternative suppliers. “It's not solely dominated by” the war in Ukraine, Rubio said of US foreign policy, adding that bilateral relationships and broader economic considerations also mattered. He said Washington was close to a trade deal with India, another factor in the administration's calculations as it sought to balance energy policy and geopolitical priorities. Rubio Backs Jac

https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-russia-t.body: Ukraine Trump Defends Russia Sanctions Waivers, Zelenskyy Says Kyiv Attacked Without Early Warning From Partners By RFE/RL October 19, 2026 00:52 CET Trump Defends Russia Sanctions Waivers, Zelenskyy Says Kyiv Attacked Without Early Warning From Partners Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Employees check medicines at a damaged pharmacy near a metro station that was hit during a Russian missile strike on Kyiv overnight on October 19. President Donald Trump slammed his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy and defended his decision to waive sweeping sanctions planned against Russia as an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table amid strong criticism from Kyiv and some US lawmakers that it sends the wrong message to the Kremlin. In a social media post on October 18, Trump blamed Zelenskyy for a lack of willingness to end Russia's war against his country, claiming that he "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." Following Trump's latest war of words against the Ukrainian leader, volleys of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles and attack drones struck targets in Kyiv and other parts of the country, killing at least two people and injuring several others. Zelenskky noted that Russia had damaged more than 10 energy facilities in overnight attacks, leaving more than half a million people without electricity as "once again, there was no early warning from our partners." Ukraine's military later said the first wave of strikes came without warning, while alerts about a second wave were received. Last week Kyiv also said there had been no warning from the United States of similar strikes, leaving little time for residents to take shelter. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, attending a meeting of Central Asian countries in Uzbekistan, denied on October 19 that there had been any suspension of intelligence sharing with Ukraine. "There has been no pause," Rubio told reporters in Uzbekistan when asked about Ukraine's claims, calling on Zelensky to "focus" on ending the war with Russia. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russian attacks on the capital killed a 21-year-old woman, injured several people, damaged residential buildings, a metro station, and a medical center, while no patients were present at the facility at the time of the strike. Russian military confirmed a strike on Kyiv and the surrounding region, claiming it targeted military-industrial facilities, missile and drone storage sites, and a data processing center. Trump signed an executive order late on October 16 that waives new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US senator Lindsey Graham, an ardent supporter of Ukraine, days after giving temporary relief on Russian diesel sanctions. Trump signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. But the moves in recent days to ease sanctions have sparked fierce criticism from many corners that Trump was giving the Kremlin a chance to fund its war machine, an accusation the president rejected. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social on October 18. Trump made ending Russia's war on Ukraine war a priority when he began his current term in January 2025, but Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions and talks have stalled. The Kremlin has been offering no concessions, repeatedly rejecting calls for a full cease-fire, and sticking to demands including Russian control over the territory it has been unable to seize in battle. The stalemate has seen the two sides step up attacks, with Moscow pummeling Kyiv and other major cities, along with targeting energy infrastructure, wreaking havoc on utilities just as Ukraine prepares for winter. Ukraine's armed forces, in return, have targeted Russia's refining operations to hinder its military operations. Those strikes have angered Trump, whose Republican party is engaged in a tight battle for control of both the Senate and House amid surging fuel prices that have angered many voters. SEE ALSO: Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move Zelenskyy warned of dire consequences for Ukraine if US support disappears. "If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told the NBC news show "Meet the Press" on October 18. "We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions...Because I think that it's all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States." He added that intelligence-sharing that Ukraine said had been interrupted earlier this week now appears to have been "de-blocked." "We are very thankful for this," Zelenskyy said. "Now it works." SEE ALSO: Kasparov Says Talks With Putin Pointless, War Is 'Ideological Basis' Of His Rule A week ago, as Trump unilaterally announced an energy cease-fire on social media, Zelenskyy appeared to support halting the strikes but said he expected Moscow to do the same. However, as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites continued, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv was "done" with unilaterally pausing its own. There was no indication Moscow had supported cease-fire announced by Trump. Putin, who Russian media said was visiting a command post earlier in the week, ordered the Russian military to continue its "massive and coordinated" strikes against targets in Ukraine. Trump's easing of sanctions has met with disdain from many lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in the United States, as well as from Ukraine's international partners. While Trump administration officials including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the president's actions, Republican lawmaker Don Bacon said moves helping the Kremlin "will go down as a very embarrassing chapter in U.S. history." SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy Says Russia Seeking Blackout In Ukraine After Latest Onslaught On Energy Facilities Trump's latest comments highlighted the growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over the administration's approach to Russia. Zelenskyy earlier announced he had held talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He added that Ukraine and the United States were "preparing the next steps in diplomacy" and that his country remained "ready to work constructively, honestly, and toward a real result." "Peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust," Zelenskyy said in a social media post about the talks. "We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years." https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2.body: Initial reports suggest that the police deployed excessive force to disperse a peaceful protest camp in Porto, Portugal, in the early hours of 15 October that injured 37 people, said Amnesty International in a statement today. “Reports of police violence against people peacefully protesting Portugal’s housing crisis are deeply troubling. People have the right to protest peacefully, including the right to occupy public space and including at night-time. The Portuguese authorities must respect and protect that right. “Dispersal of peaceful protests must be a last resort. Reports that police beat protesters with batons resulting in dozens of people being injured, including a person with a disability, raise serious concerns that the use of force was disproportionate,” said João Godinho Martins, Executive Director of Amnesty International Portugal. Reports that police beat protesters with batons resulting in dozens of people being injured, including a person with a disability, raise serious concerns that the use of force was disproportionate.” João Godinho Martins, Executive Director of Amnesty International Portugal On 10 October, people started to gather in Porto’s Praça D. João I to protest against the unaffordability of housing in Portugal, inspired by protests in Spain following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal . Protestors initially set up 50 tents to occupy the square and, according to media reports, described the peaceful action as “an act of political desperation”. On the morning of 12 October, Portuguese police ordered protesters to remove tents, citing an “unauthorized occupation of public property”. Police subsequently removed and confiscated the tents and belongings, according to protesters in contact with Amnesty International. The protest continued and on 12 October the activists notified Porto City Council of their intention to continue their demonstration. Porto mayor Pedro Duarte responded by saying that he would take an “absolutely uncompromising” stance against attempts to set up tents in the square. At around 2.30am on 15 October, roughly 40 police officers arrived at Praça D. João I to disperse the protest. Portuguese law includes a problematic blanket ban on night-time protests that runs contrary to the right to protest. According to activists and their lawyers, the police intervention resulted in 35 people sustaining minor injuries and two people sustaining serious injuries, including head injuries, a broken arm and a broken wrist. A person with a disability was among those injured. Portuguese media also reported that several people were taken to hospital. The Porto fire service reportedly assisted eight people in total and transferred two to hospital. Tomás Varela, a protester who received treatment at Santo António Hospital, reported being struck on the head with a baton and requiring nine stitches. The police described the operation as a “heavy-handed intervention” and said it was prompted by protesters’ resistance to removing the tents. “From evidence we have verified online and from interviewing protesters and witnesses at the scene, Amnesty International is concerned that the Portuguese police used excessive (and thus unlawful) force against peaceful protesters. “The Portuguese authorities must ensure an independent, impartial and effective investigation into the police operation. Anyone found responsible for unlawful use of force must be held accountable. The authorities must also fully protect the right to protest, including at night-time,” said João Godinho Martins. Background Portugal is one of the European countries most affected by the housing crisis. House prices hit a new high in 2025 , and were the highest in the eurozone. In Lisbon, the share of salary spent on rent is 116% meaning rent surpasses the average salary by 16%. Access to affordable housing continues to be a serious and persistent problem, with almost 13% of the Portuguese population living in overcrowded households . The right to housing is enshrined in Article 65 of the Portuguese Constitution which states that “everyone has the right, for themselves and their family, to housing of an adequate size, in conditions of hygiene and comfort, and which preserves personal privacy and family privacy”. The right to adequate housing is also enshrined in the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, to which Portugal is a state party. Affordability is a key component of the right to adequate housing.

The new proposals to change the ethical framework governing Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global could significantly weaken independent human rights oversight, reduce transparency and make it harder to exclude companies linked to serious abuses, Amnesty International said today. Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, is reviewing its ethical governance framework. The Gjedrem Committee, set up for this purpose, has proposed weakening the independent Council on Ethics, allowing some of its assessments to remain confidential, and making it harder to exclude companies linked to serious human rights risks. “The proposed ethical governance changes in the Norwegian fund risk weakening accountability and integrity and dismantling key human rights protections and amount to the most significant weakening of its human rights safeguards in two decades. When the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway’s borders. Other investors pay attention, and companies do too,” said John Peder Egenæs, Secretary General of Amnesty International Norway. “Under the new proposals, the Council on Ethics would lose its ability to recommend exclusion, while some companies could remain in the portfolio despite serious human rights risks and failed engagement efforts. This risks weakening independent ethical scrutiny precisely when it is most needed and making certain investments too big to exclude. This is a dangerous approach and in practice imply that companies at risk of contributing to serious violations of international law are never excluded from the fund.” When the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway’s borders. Other investors pay attention, and companies do too. John Peder Egenæs, Secretary General of Amnesty International Norway Greater discretion demands greater scrutiny The new proposals recommend that the Council of Ethics would continue to assess the risk of companies contributing to or being responsible for serious ethical violations, but without recommending exclusion or observation. Instead, the central bank of Norway, the Norges Bank (NBIM), would determine the response. The proposals also allow the Council’s risk assessments to be withheld from public disclosure where specified conditions relating to the fund’s economic interests or NBIM’s ability to fulfil its management responsibilities are met. This is a major setback for transparency, integrity and accountability. “First, the watchdog loses its teeth. Then the curtains are drawn. The fund belongs to the Norwegian people, yet they risk losing access to information about any serious abuses that their money could be linked to,” said Egenæs. While limited confidentiality during company engagement may sometimes be justified, the public must still be able to scrutinize why NBIM retains investments in companies linked to serious human rights risks. “The Norwegian people have a right to know what the bank is asking companies to change, whether those changes are actually implemented, and why it continues to invest when serious human rights risks remain,” said Egenæs. First, the watchdog loses its teeth. Then the curtains are drawn. The fund belongs to the Norwegian people, yet they risk losing access to information about any serious abuses that their money could be linked to. John Peder Egenæs Technology suppliers’ ongoing role must be examined The Gjedrem Committee report recognizes that cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data analysis can be used in surveillance, intelligence gathering and military targeting, but proposes that sales of generic products should normally fall outside conduct-based exclusion criteria. For major technology companies, the committee states that diversification considerations may carry decisive weight when assessing exclusion. “Military use alone is insufficient to establish a company’s involvement in human rights abuses. But civilian applications cannot be used to avoid scrutiny of the role technology may play in any serious rights violations. Too often, the dual-use nature of these technologies is invoked to avoid meaningful scrutiny of the risks they create,” said Egenæs. “The fund must examine what the supplier knows, how its services are used, and what it does to prevent or stop the misuse. There is an important distinction between selling a standard product and continuing to operate, adapt and support services used in serious abuses.” Engagement cannot justify indefinite delay Under the proposed framework, engagement with the company in order to address ethical concerns would replace exclusion as the primary response when risks of serious ethical violations are identified. NBIM would be required to exclude a company only where engagement has failed or has no realistic prospect of succeeding within a reasonable time, unless exclusion would limit the fund’s ability to remain broadly diversified globally. This exception risks allowing financial considerations to override human rights concerns. It also risks weakening the fund’s leverage over companies. “An abuse does not become less serious because a company is large or an investment profitable. Applying the same ethical standard means little if the fund can retain the investment after efforts to secure change have failed,” said Egenæs. “Engagement is a tool, not an end in itself. Without a credible possibility of exclusion, engagement risks becoming a conversation without consequences. In situations of armed conflict or occupation, the urgency of protecting people must guide the response. An ongoing dialogue is not, by itself, evidence that risks are being reduced.” An abuse does not become less serious because a company is large or an investment profitable. John Peder Egenæs Weapons safeguards would be weakened The committee further proposes an exception to the nuclear weapons exclusion criterion for producers based in states that are both recognized nuclear-weapon states under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and NATO allies of Norway. This would allow certain producers based in the United States, the United Kingdom and France to become eligible for investment. “The catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons – the most inhumane and destructive weapons ever to be created – do not change with the nationality of their producer. Norway’s alliances must not determine which nuclear weapons producers the fund considers acceptable investments; all companies involved must be excluded,” said Egenæs. The committee also recommends removing the specific criterion addressing arms sales to states that use those weapons to commit serious and systematic violations of international humanitarian law. It proposes retaining the criterion concerning serious violations of individuals’ rights in war and conflict, and expanding a separate criterion concerning arms sales to states subject to sanctions or arms embargoes supported by Norway. “These remaining safeguards matter. But removing an explicit criterion addressing arms transfers used in serious violations of international humanitarian law risks weakening scrutiny of suppliers and the human rights impacts of their products,” said Egenæs. Amnesty International is calling on the Norwegian government and parliament to ensure and maintain strong, independent, ethical oversight of the fund, ensure meaningful public transparency and participation and preserve exclusion as a vital safeguard when engagement cannot effectively mitigate serious human rights risks. The revised framework must be grounded in the United Nations Convention against Corruption, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct, including risk-based and heightened human rights due diligence in conflict-affected settings. “Human rights and independent oversig

Reacting to the growing number of reports that peaceful activists protesting the school hijab ban have been detained and that an activist who attempted to organize free online lessons for girls affected by the uniform regulations has gone missing, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said: “Mass arrests of peaceful protesters alongside participants in violent riots, including the reported detention of a mother protesting against her daughter’s exclusion from school, and the disappearance of an activist who aimed to help affected girls, are typical of the state’s violent suppression of the lawful exercise of the right to protest peacefully, and the crackdown on freedom of expression and all dissent in Azerbaijan. “Denying girls access to classrooms because they wear a hijab is discriminatory and violates their rights to education, and the freedoms of religion and expression. The secular character of public education doesn’t justify a blanket restriction on religious dress. Denying girls access to classrooms because they wear a hijab is discriminatory and violates their rights to education, and the freedoms of religion and expression Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director “The Azerbaijani authorities must reverse these discriminatory restrictions and ensure that affected pupils and teachers can return to school. They must immediately and unconditionally release anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights. They must respect the right to peaceful protest and all human rights.” Background According to new school uniform regulations, from 12 October, pupils and teachers wearing hijabs were denied entry to schools across Azerbaijan, prompting mass protests and acts of public disobedience, some of them resulting in violence. On that day, according to the Interior Ministry, 37 people were detained in Baku alone, while activists reported more than 200 detentions. Simultaneously, users reported that TikTok and Instagram became inaccessible in Azerbaijan. While most of the detained were shortly released, the total number of people remaining in custody is unknown. Among the known cases is Gudrat Abdullayev, who has been placed under administrative arrest for 25 days for a TikTok post, and Rafael Huseynzade, detained for 30 days after writing “Freedom for the hijab!” on a school building. On 13 October, six minors were detained on suspicion of attempting to set fire to a school. A criminal case was opened under Article 233 of the Criminal Code, concerning the organization of actions that disrupt public order or active participation in them. Officially, no one has been arrested in connection with this case so far. On 14 October, Aga Huseynov, a Muslim activist, reported the arrest of his wife, Shahizyar Huseynova, detained the previous day after protesting outside a school in Baku after their daughter was refused access. According to him, she has been detained for four months and the charges against her have not been provided. Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who had launched a free online platform connecting volunteer teachers with children excluded from school, including for wearing hijabs, went missing on 14 October after leaving his Baku home accompanied by unidentified people.

Responding to the dramatic escalation of armed hostilities between the Huthi de facto authorities, the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia in recent weeks and the growing toll on civilians amidst ongoing attacks, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said: “The risks to civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia are rapidly increasing each day this conflict escalates. All parties to the conflict must ensure civilians are protected and abide by their obligations under international humanitarian law. “Over the past week, deadly Huthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have caused significant civilian harm, including a 10 October attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds more- the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in over a decade. The attack came amidst the return of full-blown armed hostilities to Yemen with devastating consequences for civilians there, particularly on the coast and around Ta’iz, Yemen’s third largest city. Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation. Heba Morayef, Amnesty International “Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation. The deliberate targeting of civilians or civilian infrastructure, including civilian airports, is prohibited under international humanitarian law and can amount to a war crime. “All warring parties must immediately refrain from carrying out direct attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks. “In Yemen, where civilians are already grappling with a severe humanitarian crisis and the impact of years of sporadic bouts of fighting, the conflict will further compound the suffering of the civilian population. It is critical that parties to the conflict take all feasible precautions to avoid or, in any event, minimize harm to civilians and civilian objects, and provide unfettered access to humanitarian aid for civilians in need.” Background Recent weeks have seen a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the Huthi de-facto authorities in Yemen, the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. The renewed conflict in Yemen is linked to the regional conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran. The Huthis are supported by Iran and the Yemeni government by Saudi Arabia. The escalation in Yemen follows the breakdown of a UN-brokered ceasefire in July 2026, following air strikes on Sana’a airport claimed by the internationally recognized government. Between 2015 and 2022, Amnesty International documented gross human rights violations and serious violations of international humanitarian law, including likely war crimes, committed by parties to the conflict, including the Huthi armed group and Saudi-led coalition. The escalation has been accompanied by intensified ground fighting between the Huthis and Yemeni government forces inside Yemen, including deadly attacks by Huthi forces on civilian areas. While the real death toll is significantly higher, the UN human rights office reported in late September that it had documented at least 32 civilians, including 15 children, killed since August. Huthi forces have also carried out attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, as well as ships at sea. Between 5 and 11 October, Huthi attacks on civilian airports across Saudi Arabia damaged passenger terminals and civilian aircraft and killed at least 20 people and injured more than 350 people, according to the National. Saudi Arabia has also resumed its air strikes in Yemen. According to the Yemen Data Project, at least 66 civilians have been killed and 90 injured. The latest escalation is exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis in Yemen where, according to UN figures, at least 18.3 million people are acutely food insecure and more than 2.2 million children under five and 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished. Access to food and healthcare have repeatedly worsened due to the conflict, warring party conduct and humanitarian funding cuts .

https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-russia-w.body: News Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move By RFE/RL October 18, 2026 12:36 CET Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Gas prices at a Shell gas station are displayed outside of the Marathon Petroleum Corp. Los Angeles Refinery in Carson, California, on September 22. Energy analysts have questioned whether the recent diesel deal would significantly lower prices for American consumers. Ukrainian officials sharply criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping planned sanctions against Russia, saying that it "sends the wrong message to the aggressor" and "helps only the Russians." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration needed up to 60 days to assess the potential economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs, while the White House argued that imposing them immediately could hinder efforts to negotiate a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. "If Russians are cheering yesterday's decisions in the US, it is certainly not about effective pressure to end the war," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on October 17. "Indecisiveness sends the wrong signal to the aggressor. It only prolongs the war." He added that "Lindsey Graham understood this well," referring to the late senator of South Carolina for whom the sanctions legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- was named. Graham, who died on July 11, was a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine. The bill passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and was signed into law by Trump in September. But in an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18. The move prompted sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate. SEE ALSO: Trump Waives Graham Act Sanctions On Russia Before They Take Effect Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said removing the sanctions "definitely helps only the Russians." "The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X on October 17. The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions. Rubio defended the White House's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia on October 17, saying Washington needed time to assess the economic consequences of additional penalties as conflicts across several regions strain global energy supplies. Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a series of diplomatic and trade talks in Central Asia, Rubio defended the administration's efforts to balance pressure on Moscow against economic concerns. The waiver followed a diesel deal Trump announced with Russia on October 9 that prompted criticism that Washington was prioritizing domestic fuel prices over efforts to constrain the Kremlin's war against Ukraine. Zelenskyy called the waiver was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed." SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy Says Russia Seeking Blackout In Ukraine After Latest Onslaught On Energy Facilities "At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X . "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking." A senior envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, praised the waiver as "a truly historic moment." Kirill Dmitriev, who heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, wrote on X late on October 16 that "economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations." Energy Costs Complicate Russia Sanctions Rubio said the administration needed 60 days to assess the effects of sanctions and tariffs, including their potential impact on countries such as India, which continues to rely substantially on Russian energy despite efforts to diversify its supplies. He pointed to disruptions involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement, and the war between Russia and Ukraine as factors putting pressure on global energy markets. "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," Rubio said. The United States was paying higher prices than it wanted, he said, while some other countries were approaching a crisis over energy costs and availability. Rubio also defended the administration's diesel deal with Russia -- which Zelenskyy called "a gift" to Putin -- arguing the fuel would have reached international markets regardless of whether the United States purchased it. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," he said. Energy analysts have questioned whether the deal would significantly lower prices for American consumers, while warning that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with substantial economic benefits. The waiver blocks additional sanctions and tariffs approved by Congress to discourage major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, although existing sanctions remain in place. The decision drew sharp criticism from both parties. Republican Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible," while Senator John Cornyn said the late senator Graham "would be appalled." Democratic lawmakers also accused Trump of helping Russia finance its war.
